He used his position to help bring the Council of Trent to its conclusion in 1563 and worked on the Roman Catechism that followed it.

After the sudden death of his elder brother he chose to be ordained a priest and bishop, and he went to live in his diocese of Milan, which had not had a resident archbishop for decades. He visited every parish, held synods, founded seminaries for the training of priests, set up schools of Christian doctrine for children, and reformed the life of clergy and religious. He gave much of his wealth to the poor.

During the plague of 1576 he stayed in the city when many officials fled, organised care for the sick, sold his own possessions to feed the people and walked in penitential processions. He died on 3 November 1584, aged forty-six, worn out by work. He was canonised in 1610.
lessons: Reform begins with oneself
Charles first changed his own life of privilege into one of prayer and simplicity, and only then reformed others.
A shepherd stays with the flock
In the plague he did not flee; he stayed to serve the sick and the dying.
Teaching the faith matters
His schools of Christian doctrine and seminaries show that the Church is renewed when the faith is taught well.
stories: In 1569 some members of a religious order he was reforming hired a man who fired at Charles while he knelt at evening prayer. The bullet struck him but did not wound him, and he continued his prayer. He asked for leniency for his attackers.
quotes: Be sure that you first preach by the way you live; otherwise people will notice that you say one thing and live another.
St Charles Borromeo, sermon at his last synod (Office of Readings, 4 November), in substance
p
charlesborromeo.prayer: Lord, keep in your people the spirit which filled St Charles Borromeo, so that your Church may be constantly renewed and, conformed to Christ, may show his face to the world. Amen.

points: Charles first changed his own life of privilege before he reformed his diocese.
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). In the plague Charles stayed when others fled.
Seminaries and catechism classes were his answer to a confused Church. Our answer too is formation.
homily: Dear friends, Charles Borromeo had everything the world admires: noble birth, wealth, power, a cardinal's hat at twenty-one. He could have lived a comfortable life in Rome. Instead he chose to become what Jesus calls a good shepherd, one who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

He began with himself: prayer, fasting, simplicity. Then he went to live among his people in Milan, visited every parish, founded seminaries and catechism schools, and reformed what was corrupt. When the plague came in 1576 and officials fled, he stayed, sold his goods to feed the hungry and walked barefoot in penitential processions.

The Church is always in need of renewal, and renewal always begins with one heart. Let us pray for our bishops and priests, that they may be shepherds like Charles. And let each of us ask: what in my own life needs reform before I ask others to change? Amen.

leogreat.t: Pope and Doctor of the Church
word: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
Matthew 16:18
life: Leo was probably born in Tuscany or in Rome near the end of the fourth century. As a deacon of the Roman Church he was already trusted with important tasks, and while he was on a mission in Gaul in 440 he was elected Bishop of Rome. He served as Pope for twenty-one years, until his death on 10 November 461.

Leo defended the true faith about Christ. In 449 he wrote a letter, known as the Tome, to Flavian, Patriarch of Constantinople, explaining that in the one Person of Jesus Christ the divine and human natures are united without confusion and without division. At the Council of Chalcedon in 451 the bishops welcomed the letter, and the Council's acts record their acclamation that Peter had spoken through Leo.

He was also a shepherd in dangerous times. In 452 he went out to meet Attila the Hun in northern Italy, and Attila turned back. In 455 he persuaded Genseric the Vandal to spare the people of Rome from burning and massacre. Nearly a hundred of his sermons survive, especially on the feasts of Christ. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1754.
lessons: Know the faith clearly
Leo shows that loving Christ includes knowing who he is: true God and true man.
Courage in crisis
He faced invading armies with prayer and the authority of his office, not with weapons.
Preach the feasts
His sermons help the faithful enter the mysteries of Christmas, Lent, Easter and Pentecost.
stories: In 452 Leo, with two Roman officials, met Attila near Mantua, and the Huns withdrew from Italy. Later tradition added that Attila saw the apostles Peter and Paul standing beside the Pope.
quotes: Christian, remember your dignity.
St Leo the Great, Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord (Office of Readings, 25 December)
leogreat.prayer: God our Father, you built your Church on the rock of Peter's faith. Through the prayers of Pope St Leo the Great, keep us firm in the truth and united in your love. Amen.

points: True God and true man, one Person: Leo's Tome gave the Church clear words for its faith.
You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18). Leo served unity as Peter's successor.
Leo's Christmas cry: Christian, remember your dignity. Live as one who shares the life of God.
homily: Dear friends, Pope Leo the Great lived in a time of confusion and danger. Inside the Church people argued about who Christ is; outside, the Huns and the Vandals threatened Rome. Leo answered both with the same weapons: truth and prayer.

To the confusion he gave clarity: Jesus Christ is one Person, truly God and truly man, without mixture and without division. The bishops at Chalcedon, hearing his letter, said that Peter had spoken through Leo. Jesus had told Peter: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18). Leo served that rock.

And to every Christian he gave a sentence we hear each Christmas: Christian, remember your dignity. Because God became man, we share in the life of God. Let us not live beneath that dignity. Today let us know our faith a little better, read one page of the Catechism, and thank God for the gift of the Church's unity. Amen.

martintours.t: Soldier, monk and Bishop of Tours
word: I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.
Matthew 25:36
life: Martin was born around 316 at Sabaria in Pannonia (today Szombathely in Hungary), the son of a Roman army officer, and grew up in Pavia in Italy. Drawn to Christ as a boy, he became a catechumen, but as an officer's son he was enrolled in the army at fifteen. His life was written by his friend Sulpicius Severus, who knew him personally.

At Amiens, on a freezing winter day, Martin cut his military cloak in two and gave half to a poor man begging at the city gate. That night, Sulpicius tells us, he saw Christ in a dream wearing the half-cloak and saying that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Martin was baptised soon afterwards. He later left the army, saying he was now a soldier of Christ, and became a disciple of St Hilary of Poitiers. Around 361 he founded at Ligugé one of the first monasteries in Gaul.

In 371 the people of Tours made him their bishop, against his wishes. He lived as a monk at Marmoutier outside the city, travelled through the countryside preaching to the rural people, and cared for the poor and prisoners. He died at Candes on 8 November 397 and was buried at Tours on 11 November. He was one of the first saints honoured who was not a martyr.
lessons: Share what you have
Martin did not give the whole cloak; he gave what he could at once, and Christ accepted it as given to himself.
Seeing Christ in the poor
His dream is a living commentary on Matthew 25: whatever we do to the least, we do to Christ.
Humble authority
Even as a bishop he kept the simple life of a monk and served the people himself.
stories: At the gate of Amiens Martin shared his cloak with a freezing beggar and that night saw Christ wearing it. The story comes from his contemporary biographer Sulpicius Severus.
A later legend says that Martin hid in a goose pen to avoid being made bishop, but the cackling geese gave him away. This is why goose is eaten on St Martin's Day in parts of Europe.
quotes: Lord, if your people still need me, I do not refuse the work; your will be done.
St Martin of Tours on his deathbed, as reported by Sulpicius Severus, in substance
p
martintours.prayer: Lord God, St Martin of Tours glorified you by his life and by his death. Renew in our hearts the wonders of your grace, so that neither life nor death may separate us from your love. Amen.

points: Martin gave what he could at that moment. Generosity does not wait until we have plenty.
I was naked and you clothed me (Matthew 25:36). That night Martin saw Christ wearing his cloak.
He left one army to serve another: a monk and bishop who kept the simple life and served the poor himself.
homily: Dear friends, on a freezing day at the gate of Amiens a young Roman soldier saw a beggar shivering. He had no money with him, only his military cloak. So he took his sword, cut the cloak in two, and gave half away. That night, his biographer tells us, Martin saw Christ in a dream wearing that half-cloak.

Jesus had said: I was naked and you gave me clothing (Matthew 25:36). Martin did not give the whole cloak; he gave what he could at that moment, and Christ received it as given to himself. Generosity does not wait until we have plenty. It begins with the half-cloak we have now.

Martin later became a monk and a bishop, yet he kept the simple life of a monk and went himself to the poor and the prisoners. Let us be like him this week: give one warm garment, one meal, one hour of company to someone in need, and remember whom we are really clothing. Amen.

josaphat.t: Eastern Catholic Archbishop of Polotsk, martyr for the unity of the Church
word: That they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
John 17:21
life: John Kuntsevych was born around 1580 in Volodymyr in Volhynia (in present-day Ukraine), in a family of the Byzantine rite. In 1596, by the Union of Brest, many bishops of the Ruthenian Church entered into full communion with Rome while keeping their own Eastern liturgy and traditions. As a young man John embraced this union with conviction.

In 1604 he became a monk of the Order of St Basil at the monastery of the Holy Trinity in Vilnius, taking the name Josaphat. He was known for his prayer, his fasting and his preaching. He became archimandrite, and in 1618 Archbishop of Polotsk. He restored churches, taught the catechism, cared for the poor and worked tirelessly to bring Christians of his region into the unity of the Catholic Church while defending the Eastern liturgy.

Feelings ran high among those who opposed the union. On 12 November 1623, in Vitebsk, a mob broke into his residence and killed him. He was beatified in 1643 and canonised in 1867, the first Eastern Catholic to be canonised through a formal process of the Roman Curia. Since 1963 his relics have rested in St Peter's Basilica in Rome.
lessons: Unity is worth a life
Josaphat lived and died for Christ's prayer that all may be one.
Eastern and Catholic
He shows that one can be fully Catholic while keeping one's own Eastern liturgy and heritage; a lesson dear to the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Churches.
Love even the enemy
Tradition remembers that he asked his people not to harm his attackers.
stories: Josaphat was killed in Vitebsk in 1623 by opponents of the Union of Brest, and his body was thrown into the river Dvina. It was later recovered and venerated.
josaphat.prayer: Lord, stir up in your Church the Spirit that filled St Josaphat when he laid down his life for the sheep. Through his prayers, may we be strengthened by the same Spirit and not be afraid to give our lives for others. Amen.

points: That they may all be one
Jesus prayed for the unity of his disciples (John 17:21). Josaphat gave his life for that prayer.
He kept the Byzantine liturgy while living in full communion with Peter: a mirror for the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Churches.
Tradition remembers that he asked his people not to harm those who came to kill him.
homily: Dear friends, on the night before he died Jesus prayed: that they may all be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that the world may believe (John 17:21). Division among Christians wounds that prayer. St Josaphat gave his life to heal it.

He was a monk and archbishop of the Byzantine tradition who embraced full communion with the Bishop of Rome while keeping his Eastern liturgy, spirituality and customs. For us in Kerala this is a familiar story: the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Churches are fully Catholic and proudly Eastern. Josaphat shows that this is not a compromise but a gift.

Opponents of unity killed him in 1623. Tradition says he asked his people not to harm his attackers. Let us pray today for the unity of all Christians, love our own liturgical tradition, and refuse to speak with contempt of any other Church. Unity begins in the way we speak. Amen.

albertgreat.t: Dominican bishop, Doctor of the Church, patron of scientists
word: O Lord, how manifold are your works! In wisdom you have made them all; the earth is full of your creatures.
Psalm 104:24
life: Albert was born around 1200 at Lauingen in Swabia (Germany). While studying at Padua he met the Dominicans and entered the Order of Preachers. He taught in several German houses, then in Paris and in Cologne, where he founded a great house of studies.

Albert studied everything: Scripture, theology and philosophy, but also plants, animals, minerals and the stars. He made the works of Aristotle known to Christian scholars and showed that faith and reason are friends, not enemies. Among his students was a quiet young Dominican, Thomas Aquinas, whose genius Albert recognised and defended.

From 1260 to 1262 he was Bishop of Regensburg, then resigned to return to teaching and preaching. In old age he travelled to Paris to defend the teaching of Thomas after his death. Albert died in Cologne on 15 November 1280. He was canonised and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931, and in 1941 Pius XII named him patron of those who study the natural sciences.
lessons: Faith and reason together
Albert studied creation with wonder because it is the work of God's wisdom.
A good teacher lifts others
He rejoiced in the gifts of his student Thomas and helped him grow.
Humility in greatness
He gave up the office of bishop to return to study, prayer and teaching.
stories: Tradition says that fellow students called the silent Thomas Aquinas the dumb ox, and Albert answered that one day this ox would bellow so loudly that the whole world would hear him.
albertgreat.prayer: Lord God, you made St Albert great by his gift of joining human wisdom to divine faith. Help us so to follow his teaching that every advance in knowledge may lead us to know and love you more. Amen.

points: How manifold are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you made them all (Psalm 104:24). Albert studied creation with wonder.
Science and faith both seek truth; the same God is author of both.
Albert recognised and defended the genius of his student Thomas Aquinas.
homily: Dear friends, St Albert the Great studied plants, animals, stones and stars, and he also studied Scripture and theology. He saw no conflict between them. With the psalmist he could say: how manifold are your works, O Lord; in wisdom you have made them all (Psalm 104:24). Every discovery about creation is a discovery about the Creator's wisdom.

Today many young people are told that they must choose between faith and science. Albert, patron of scientists, says no: truth cannot contradict truth, because the same God is the author of nature and of revelation. Let our students study hard and pray hard.

Albert was also a great teacher. When others laughed at the silent Thomas Aquinas, Albert saw his genius and protected it. Parents and teachers, look for the hidden gifts in your children and encourage them. And all of us, let us look at creation today with wonder and thank its Maker. Amen.

elizabethhungary.t: Princess, wife, mother and servant of the poor
word: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
Luke 6:36
life: Elizabeth was born in 1207, a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary. As a child she was sent to the court of Thuringia in Germany, and in 1221 she married Ludwig IV, Landgrave of Thuringia. Their marriage was a happy one; they had three children, and Ludwig supported her generosity to the poor.

From the Wartburg castle Elizabeth went down to the sick and hungry, fed hundreds of people daily during a famine, and built a hospital at the foot of the castle. In 1227 Ludwig died of illness at Otranto in southern Italy while on his way to the Crusade. Elizabeth, only twenty, was grief-stricken; she said that the world and all its joys were dead to her with him.

Soon afterwards she left the court, became a member of the Franciscan Third Order and used her dowry to found a hospital at Marburg, where she herself nursed the sick, the poor and lepers. Under a strict spiritual director, Konrad of Marburg, she lived in poverty and penance. Worn out, she died on 17 November 1231, aged twenty-four. She was canonised in 1235.
lessons: Holiness in marriage
Elizabeth loved her husband and children deeply; her sanctity grew within family life.
Riches are for sharing
A princess, she saw her wealth as belonging to the poor.
Faith in sorrow
After the death of her husband she turned grief into deeper service.
stories: A legend says that once, when Elizabeth was carrying bread in her cloak to the poor, she was stopped and asked what she carried; when she opened her cloak, only roses were seen.
Elizabeth founded the hospital of St Francis at Marburg in 1229 and personally served the sick there until her death.
elizabethhungary.prayer: God of mercy, you gave St Elizabeth of Hungary the grace to recognise and honour Christ in the poor. Through her prayers, make us untiring servants of the hungry and the afflicted. Amen.

points: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful (Luke 6:36). Elizabeth fed hundreds daily in famine.
She loved her husband and children deeply; her sanctity grew inside marriage.
Widowed at twenty, she founded a hospital and nursed the sick herself.
homily: Dear friends, St Elizabeth of Hungary was a princess who lived only twenty-four years, yet she is one of the best-loved saints of Europe. Why? Because she took seriously the word of Jesus: be merciful, just as your Father is merciful (Luke 6:36).

She was a loving wife and mother. Her husband Ludwig supported her charity, and together they made their castle a place from which bread went down to the hungry. Holiness did not take her away from family life; it grew inside it. When Ludwig died, she was crushed with grief, but she turned her sorrow into service, founding a hospital at Marburg and nursing the sick and lepers with her own hands.

Elizabeth teaches families that holiness is possible at home, and teaches those who grieve that love can still be given. Today let us share bread with someone who is hungry, and pray for families who have lost a husband or wife. Amen.

cecilia.t: Virgin and martyr of Rome, patron of music
word: O sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.
Psalm 96:1
life: Cecilia is one of the most honoured martyrs of the early Roman Church. Her name is said in the Roman Canon of the Mass (Eucharistic Prayer I), and an ancient church in the Trastevere district of Rome bears her name. These facts show that her memory was treasured from early times.

The details of her life come from a later account, the Acts of St Cecilia, written around the late fifth century, which historians regard as largely legendary. It tells that Cecilia, a Christian girl of a noble family, had consecrated her virginity to God but was given in marriage to a young pagan, Valerian. She told him of the angel who guarded her; Valerian was converted and baptised, together with his brother Tiburtius, and both died as martyrs.

According to the same account Cecilia was then arrested; she survived an attempt to suffocate her and, after being struck with a sword, lived for three days, encouraging the faithful, before she died. In 1599 her tomb in Santa Cecilia was opened, and the sculptor Stefano Maderno carved the well-known statue of her lying on her side.
lessons: Belonging wholly to God
Cecilia's story shows a heart given entirely to Christ.
Bringing others to faith
Her witness led her husband and his brother to Christ.
Singing in the heart
She is patron of music because the account says that, while instruments played at her wedding, she sang to God in her heart.
stories: The Acts say that at her wedding feast, while the instruments played, Cecilia sang in her heart to God alone, asking that her heart be kept pure. From this phrase she became patron of musicians.
When her tomb was opened in 1599, Stefano Maderno sculpted the figure of the martyr lying as she was found; the statue lies beneath the altar of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere.
cecilia.prayer: Lord, accept our prayer through the intercession of St Cecilia, and let us sing your praises with our lives as well as our lips. Amen.

points: Cecilia's story shows a heart given entirely to Christ.
Sing to the Lord a new song (Psalm 96:1). She sang to God in her heart while the world made noise around her.
Her witness brought her husband and his brother to faith.
homily: Dear friends, St Cecilia is one of the martyrs named in the ancient Roman Canon of the Mass. Much of her story comes to us through a later account that historians regard as largely legendary, and we say so honestly. Yet the Church has loved her memory from the earliest centuries, and her story carries a true message.

The account says that at her wedding feast, while the instruments played, Cecilia sang in her heart to God alone. That is why she is patron of music. The psalm invites us: sing to the Lord a new song (Psalm 96:1). Amid the noise of our world, can we keep a song to God in our hearts?
Her faith also led her husband and his brother to Christ. Let us thank God today for our choirs and musicians, who help us pray, and let us sing to the Lord with our lives as well as our lips. Amen.

word: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
Romans 8:35
life: The Gospel reached Vietnam in the sixteenth century, and the Church grew among the people. From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century Christians suffered repeated waves of persecution; historians estimate that well over a hundred thousand were killed for their faith.

On 19 June 1988 Pope St John Paul II canonised 117 of these martyrs, who died between 1745 and 1862: 96 Vietnamese, 11 Spanish Dominicans and 10 French missionaries of the Paris Foreign Missions Society. They included 8 bishops, 50 priests and 59 lay people: catechists, soldiers, farmers, fishermen, a physician, and fathers and mothers of families.

Andrew Dũng-Lạc, a Vietnamese diocesan priest, was arrested several times; his parishioners paid ransoms for his release. He was beheaded in Hanoi on 21 December 1839. Another, St Paul Lê Bảo Tịnh, wrote from prison a letter describing his sufferings and his joy in Christ; it is read in the Office of Readings on this day.
lessons: Faith of ordinary people
Most of these martyrs were lay people: parents, farmers, soldiers and catechists.
The Church of Asia
Their witness reminds Indian Christians that Asia has its own great martyrs.
Courage that encourages
The letters from prison strengthened those still free.
stories: In 1843 St Paul Lê Bảo Tịnh wrote that his prison was like an image of hell, with chains, cruelty and hunger, but that in the midst of these torments Christ was with him and filled him with joy. He asked his fellow Christians to pray that he would remain faithful.
quotes: In the midst of these torments, which usually terrify others, I am, by the grace of God, full of joy and gladness, because I am not alone; Christ is with me.
St Paul Lê Bảo Tịnh, letter from prison (1843), Office of Readings, 24 November, in substance
p
vietnamesemartyrs.prayer: O God, source of all fatherhood, you kept the martyrs Andrew Dũng-Lạc and his companions faithful to the cross of your Son even to the shedding of their blood. Through their prayers, help us to spread your love among our brothers and sisters. Amen.

points: Who will separate us from the love of Christ (Romans 8:35)? Not prison, not torture, not the sword.
Most of the 117 were lay people: farmers, soldiers, catechists, parents.
Their witness reminds Indian Christians that our continent has its own great saints.
homily: Dear friends, St Paul asks: who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword (Romans 8:35)? The martyrs of Vietnam answered with their lives: no one and nothing.

Between 1745 and 1862 tens of thousands of Vietnamese Christians died for the faith; 117 of them were canonised in 1988. Most were not priests or religious but lay people: farmers, fishermen, soldiers, catechists, fathers and mothers. From prison St Paul Lê Bảo Tịnh wrote that in the midst of torments he was full of joy, because Christ was with him.

They are Asia's martyrs, our neighbours in faith. Today let us pray for Christians who are persecuted in Asia and elsewhere, and ask for the courage to be faithful in the small trials of our own lives. Amen.

catherinealex.t: Virgin and martyr, patron of students and philosophers
word: Always be ready to make your defense to anyone who demands from you an accounting for the hope that is in you.
1 Peter 3:15
life: Catherine has been honoured since at least the eighth or ninth century, especially in the East, as a learned young woman of Alexandria in Egypt who died as a martyr in the early fourth century. Her story, however, comes to us through later accounts with many legendary features, and historians cannot confirm its details. For this reason her memorial was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969; it was restored as an optional memorial in 2002.

According to the tradition, Catherine was of noble birth and highly educated. When the emperor persecuted Christians, she rebuked him and defended the faith so wisely that fifty philosophers summoned to refute her were converted instead, and were themselves martyred.

The tradition continues that she was condemned to be broken on a spiked wheel, which shattered when she touched it, and that she was then beheaded. Her body was said to have been carried by angels to Mount Sinai, where the ancient monastery bearing her name still stands. She was one of the saints whose voices St Joan of Arc said she heard.
lessons: Learning in the service of faith
Catherine is a model for students: knowledge can serve the truth of Christ.
Courage to speak
She defended the faith before the powerful with gentleness and clarity.
Honesty about sources
The Church honours her while saying plainly that much of her story is legend: devotion does not need exaggeration.
stories: The tradition says the emperor gathered fifty philosophers to defeat Catherine in debate, but her arguments led them to faith in Christ.
The spiked wheel that, according to the legend, broke at her touch gave its name to the spinning firework called a Catherine wheel.
catherinealex.prayer: Almighty God, you gave St Catherine of Alexandria wisdom and courage to confess your Son. Through her prayers, give students and teachers a love of truth and the strength to bear witness to Christ. Amen.

points: Always be ready to make your defence for the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15). Catherine is remembered for answering with wisdom.
Study in the service of faith
Students and teachers: knowledge can serve the truth of Christ.
The Church honours her while saying plainly that much is legend; faith does not need exaggeration.
homily: Dear friends, St Catherine of Alexandria has been loved for over a thousand years, especially in the East, as a young woman who defended the faith with wisdom before the powerful. The Church tells us honestly that most details of her story are legendary. That honesty is itself a lesson: our faith rests on Christ, not on exaggerated tales.

What remains is a true calling for every Christian: always be ready to make your defence to anyone who asks you for the reason of the hope that is in you, yet do it with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Catherine is remembered as one who did exactly that.

Students, she is your patron. Study well; learn your faith as seriously as your subjects; and when someone questions your belief, answer calmly and kindly. Let us pray today for all students and teachers. Amen.

andrewapostle.t: Apostle, the First-Called, brother of St Peter
word: He first found his brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which is translated Anointed).
John 1:41
life: Andrew was a fisherman from Bethsaida in Galilee who lived at Capernaum with his brother Simon. He was first a disciple of John the Baptist. When John pointed to Jesus and said, Look, here is the Lamb of God, Andrew and another disciple followed Jesus and stayed with him that day (John 1:35–39). For this reason the Eastern Churches call him the Protokletos, the First-Called.

His first act as a disciple was to bring his brother to Jesus. In the Gospels Andrew keeps bringing people to the Lord: Simon Peter (John 1:41–42), the boy with five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:8–9), and the Greeks who wished to see Jesus (John 12:20–22). With Peter, James and John he heard Jesus speak about the end of the age on the Mount of Olives (Mark 13:3).

Ancient tradition says that after Pentecost Andrew preached in the lands around the Black Sea and in Greece, and that he was crucified at Patras in Achaia. A later tradition says that his cross was X-shaped. His relics are venerated at Amalfi in Italy; in 1964 Pope St Paul VI returned the relic of his head to Patras. He is patron of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, and also of Scotland, Russia and Greece.
lessons: Bring someone to Jesus
Andrew's whole life shows that the best thing we can do for others is to introduce them to Christ.
Small gifts in the hands of Jesus
He brought five loaves and two fish, asking what they were among so many; Jesus fed thousands.
Brothers in two Churches
Andrew is patron of Constantinople as Peter is of Rome; his feast is a day of prayer for Christian unity.
stories: After a single day with Jesus, Andrew ran to tell his brother and brought him to the Lord (John 1:40–42).
An ancient account of his passion says that Andrew greeted the cross on which he was to die as the cross he had long desired, and preached from it for two days.
quotes: O good cross, long desired and now prepared for my longing soul.
Words given to St Andrew in the ancient Passion of St Andrew, in substance
p
andrewapostle.prayer: Lord, we humbly ask that St Andrew the Apostle, who was a preacher and pastor of your Church, may always be our advocate before you. Amen.

points: Andrew spent one day with Jesus and was changed (John 1:39). Faith begins with time spent with him.
His first act was to bring his brother (John 1:41). Mission begins at home.
He brought five loaves and two fish; Jesus fed thousands (John 6:8–11).
homily: Dear friends, St Andrew is called in the East the First-Called. He was a disciple of John the Baptist, and when John pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, Andrew followed. Jesus asked: what are you looking for? And then: come and see (John 1:38–39). Andrew stayed with him that day, and his life changed.

What did he do next? He ran to his brother Simon and said: we have found the Messiah; and he brought him to Jesus (John 1:41–42). Without Andrew's invitation, would there have been a St Peter? Later Andrew brought the boy with five loaves, and the Greeks who wanted to see Jesus. Andrew is the saint of bringing people.

Each of us was brought to Jesus by someone: a parent, a catechist, a friend. Today let us thank God for that person, and let us become an Andrew for someone else. Invite one person this Advent: come and see. Amen.

word: Both of them were righteous before God, living blamelessly according to all the commandments and regulations of the Lord.
Luke 1:6
life: Zechariah was a priest of the order of Abijah, and his wife Elizabeth was of the family of Aaron. Luke tells us they were righteous before God, but they had no child, and both were getting old (Luke 1:5–7). While Zechariah was serving in the Temple, the angel Gabriel appeared and told him that Elizabeth would bear a son, to be called John. Because he doubted, Zechariah was struck mute until the promise was fulfilled.

When Mary, carrying Jesus, visited her kinswoman, the child leapt in Elizabeth's womb and she, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried: blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb (Luke 1:41–42). At John's naming Zechariah's tongue was loosed and he sang the Benedictus, which the Church prays every morning (Luke 1:67–79).
lessons: Faithful in waiting
They kept praying and serving through long years without an answer.
God hears late prayers
Your prayer has been heard, the angel said: God's timing is not ours.
Praise when the tongue is loosed
Zechariah's first words after his silence were a song of praise.
stories: Elizabeth was the first to greet Jesus, hidden in Mary's womb, with the words that became the Hail Mary.

points: Holiness does not protect from sorrow; Zechariah and Elizabeth carried a painful emptiness with faith.
God answered in his time, with more than they asked: the forerunner of the Messiah.
Silence turned into praise. Let our trials end in thanksgiving.
homily: Dear friends, Zechariah and Elizabeth were good people with an unanswered prayer. Luke says they were righteous before God, yet they had no child, and in their world that was a deep sorrow. They did not stop praying or serving.

Then, when it seemed too late, the angel said: your prayer has been heard (Luke 1:13). God gave them John, who would prepare the way of the Lord. Zechariah doubted and fell silent; but when the child was named, his tongue was loosed and he sang: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel (Luke 1:68).

Some of us carry long-unanswered prayers. Let this holy couple teach us to keep our lamp burning, to keep serving, and to trust God's timing. And when the answer comes, let our first words be praise. Amen.

zechelizabeth.prayer: Lord God, you heard the prayer of Zechariah and Elizabeth and gave them John, the forerunner of your Son. Through their prayers, keep us faithful in waiting and ready to praise you. Amen.

thomasindia.n: Entrance of St Thomas the Apostle into India
thomasindia.t: Commemoration of the arrival of our Father in faith
word: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
John 20:28
life: The ancient and constant tradition of the St Thomas Christians holds that the apostle Thomas reached the coast of Malabar, traditionally at Kodungallur (Muziris) in AD 52, preached the Gospel and founded communities, remembered as the seven and a half churches. Today the Syro-Malabar Church remembers his entrance into India with gratitude.

Kerala had long trade links with the Roman world through Muziris, which makes such a journey historically possible, though the details come to us through tradition, songs such as the Thomma Parvam and the living memory of the community rather than written records of the first century.
lessons: Faith that confesses
My Lord and my God: the faith Thomas brought is the faith we profess.
A Church with an apostle's roots
We are heirs of an apostolic Church; that is a gift and a responsibility.
Mission continues
The faith that came to India by sea now goes out from India to the world.
stories: Tradition remembers that Thomas landed at Muziris in AD 52 and first preached among the Jewish community there.

points: Let us also go, that we may die with him (John 11:16): the same courage carried Thomas to India.
His great confession is the heart of the faith he planted among us.
We are called to pass on what we received.
homily: Dear friends, today we give thanks for the day, remembered in our tradition, when the apostle Thomas set foot on our land. The man who once said, let us also go, that we may die with him (John 11:16), crossed the sea to bring Christ to a people he had never seen.

He brought us the faith he had confessed before the risen Lord: my Lord and my God (John 20:28). For nearly two thousand years the St Thomas Christians have kept this faith through many trials. We are not a young Church; we stand on an apostle's foundation.

But a gift received must be handed on. Thomas came to us; now our missionaries go out from Kerala to the whole world. Let us thank God for our heritage, live our faith with joy, and support the mission of the Church by our prayer and our sacrifice. Amen.

thomasindia.prayer: Lord Jesus, you sent your apostle Thomas to our land to proclaim you as Lord and God. Keep us faithful to the faith he planted, and make us missionaries of your Gospel in our time. Amen.

presentationmary.n: The Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
presentationmary.t: Mary given to God in the Temple
word: Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!
Luke 11:28
life: An ancient tradition, recorded in the second-century Protoevangelium of James, tells that Joachim and Anne brought their daughter Mary as a little child to the Temple in Jerusalem and offered her to God. The feast was celebrated in Jerusalem from the sixth century, linked to the dedication of the New Church of St Mary in 543, and spread through the East; in the West it became universal in the late sixteenth century.

The Gospels do not narrate this event, and the Church presents it as tradition. Its meaning, however, is firm: from her earliest years Mary belonged wholly to God, preparing to become the dwelling of his Son. In the Syro-Malankara Church it is kept as the Entry of Mary, Mother of God, into the Temple.
lessons: A life given early
Mary's whole life was an offering; it is never too early to give our life to God.
Hearing and keeping the Word
Jesus called blessed those who hear God's word and keep it; Mary did this first.
Parents who give
Joachim and Anne model parents who offer their children to God.
stories: The child on the Temple steps
The Protoevangelium says the little Mary went up the Temple steps without looking back. This is a pious tradition, not Gospel history.

points: Like Hannah's Samuel, Mary was lent to the Lord. Our children too belong first to God.
Mary is blessed not only as mother but as the perfect hearer of the Word (Luke 11:28).
The child offered in the Temple became the living temple of God.
homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate an ancient tradition: little Mary brought by her parents to the Temple and given to God. The Gospels do not tell this story; it comes from tradition. But it expresses a truth the Gospels make clear: Mary belonged wholly to God from the beginning.

When a woman in the crowd praised Jesus' mother, he answered: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it (Luke 11:28). Jesus was not lowering Mary; he was showing her true greatness. She heard God's word and kept it in her heart from childhood to the Cross.

The child offered in the Temple became the temple in which God's Son dwelt. Parents, offer your children to God; children, offer your day to God. And let all of us, like Mary, hear God's word and keep it. Amen.

presentationmary.prayer: Lord God, you willed that the Blessed Virgin Mary should belong wholly to you from her childhood. Through her prayers, help us to offer our lives to you and to hear and keep your word. Amen.

nicaea318.t: Bishops of the First Ecumenical Council (AD 325)
word: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Hebrews 13:8
life: In AD 325 the bishops of the Church gathered at Nicaea, near Constantinople, to answer the teaching of Arius, who said that the Son of God was a creature. Tradition numbers the bishops as 318. Many of them bore in their bodies the scars of the recent persecutions.

The Council confessed that the Son is true God from true God, begotten not made, of one being with the Father. This confession, completed at Constantinople in 381, is the Creed we pray at every Holy Qurbono. In 2025 the whole Church marked its 1700th anniversary.
lessons: Truth worth defending
The Fathers knew that who Jesus is matters for our salvation.
Faith handed on
The Creed is a gift received; we must know it and teach it.
Unity in confession
Christians of East and West still pray the same Creed.
stories: Ancient historians tell that some bishops at Nicaea had lost an eye or the use of a hand under persecution, and that the emperor honoured their wounds.

points: Hebrews tells us to remember those who spoke God's word and to imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7).
The Son is not a creature but of one being with the Father: our salvation depends on it.
Let the words we say each Sunday become our own.
homily: Dear friends, today we remember the bishops gathered at Nicaea in 325, whom tradition numbers as 318. They met at a moment of danger, when a popular teaching said that the Son of God was only the highest of creatures.

Their answer was clear: the Son is true God from true God, begotten not made, of one being with the Father. If Jesus were not truly God, he could not unite us to God. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Hebrews 13:8).
Every Sunday we pray their Creed. Let us not say it carelessly. This week, pray it slowly once each day, and explain one line of it to your children. We are the heirs of the Fathers. Amen.

nicaea318.prayer: Lord God, you gave your Church the faith confessed at Nicaea. Through the prayers of the holy Fathers, keep us firm in that faith, and let us confess your Son as true God from true God in word and in life. Amen.

word: Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.
Revelation 2:10
life: The Eastern Churches remember on this day thirty-three Christians martyred at Melitene in Lesser Armenia (in present-day Türkiye) in the persecution under the emperor Diocletian, around AD 300. Tradition names their leader Hieron, a strong farmer from Tyana who had been forced into the army, together with thirty-two companions.

The details of their story come to us through later Eastern accounts and are best understood as tradition. What is certain is that the Church of the East kept their memory as men who refused to deny Christ when soldiers were ordered to sacrifice to idols.
lessons: Faithful together
They strengthened one another; faith is lived in community.
Ordinary men, extraordinary courage
Farmers and soldiers, not scholars, chose Christ above life.
The crown of life
Faithfulness unto death receives a crown no one can take away.
stories: Tradition says Hieron, a powerful farmer forced into the army, led his companions in refusing to offer sacrifice, and they died together.

points: The risen Christ promises the crown of life to the faithful (Revelation 2:10).
They faced death together; we need brothers and sisters in faith.
Daily faithfulness in small trials prepares us for great ones.
homily: Dear friends, today the Church remembers thirty-three men who died together for Christ at Melitene, around the year 300. They were ordinary men, farmers and soldiers, and when they were ordered to sacrifice to idols, they said no.
The risen Christ said to the Church: be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life (Revelation 2:10). These martyrs believed that promise more than the threats of the emperor.

Few of us will face such a choice. But each day we face small ones: to tell the truth when lying is easier, to defend the weak when silence is safer, to pray when we are tired. Let us strengthen one another as they did, and be faithful in little things. Amen.

melitene33.prayer: Lord Jesus, you gave the martyrs of Melitene strength to be faithful until death. Through their prayers, make us faithful in the small trials of each day and bring us to the crown of life. Amen.

word: Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
2 Timothy 2:3
life: The Malankara calendar names this saint simply as St Theodore. In the Eastern Churches the best-known Theodore is the soldier-martyr Theodore of Amasea in Pontus, called the Recruit, who was burned to death around AD 306 for refusing to sacrifice to the gods. St Gregory of Nyssa preached a sermon in his honour at his shrine, which shows how early his cult was established.

Because several saints of this name are honoured in the East, and the details of their lives come largely through later accounts, we present his story as tradition. Whatever the details, he is remembered as a soldier who served Christ before any earthly commander.
lessons: A soldier of Christ
Our first loyalty is to Christ, whatever our job or uniform.
Courage in faith
Faith sometimes requires saying no to the powerful.
The Church remembers
Gregory of Nyssa's sermon shows how the early Church treasured its martyrs.
stories: St Gregory of Nyssa preached at Theodore's shrine in Euchaita, describing pilgrims who came to pray there.

points: Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 2:3).
Theodore served the empire but obeyed Christ first.
Christians in uniform, in offices and in fields witness by honesty and courage.
homily: Dear friends, today we remember St Theodore, honoured in the East as a soldier who would not deny Christ. Paul wrote to Timothy: share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 2:3).

Theodore served in the Roman army, but when he was told to sacrifice to idols, he knew which commander came first. Tradition says he was burned for his faith around 306, and within a century pilgrims were coming to his shrine.

Many of us serve in jobs where faith is tested: in offices, police stations, hospitals, fields and markets. Let us serve honestly and well, and when we are asked to do what is wrong, let us, like Theodore, remember our first commander. Amen.

theodore.prayer: Lord Jesus, you gave St Theodore the courage to serve you before every earthly power. Through his prayers, make us faithful and honest in our work, and brave when our faith is tested. Amen.

johnalmsgiver.t: Patriarch of Alexandria, friend of the poor
word: Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and will be repaid in full.
Proverbs 19:17
life: John was born in Amathus in Cyprus in the sixth century. After his wife and children died, he gave himself wholly to God and to the poor. Around 610 he was chosen Patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt.

He made a list of the poor of the city, whom he called his masters, and provided for thousands of them; he founded hospitals and houses for travellers and helped refugees from the Persian invasion of Palestine. When the Persians approached Egypt around 619, he returned to Cyprus, where he died. His life was written soon after by Leontius of Neapolis.
lessons: The poor are our masters
John called the poor his masters, because Christ hides in them.
Generosity without calculation
He gave so freely that people said he could not be outgiven by God.
Holiness after loss
Grief over his family became love for the whole city.
stories: A story tells that a rich man gave John a costly blanket; John sold it for the poor, the man bought it back and gave it again, and John sold it again, saying they would see who tired first.

points: Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord (Proverbs 19:17).
John served the poor as one serves a master: with respect.
His loss became the source of a wider love.
homily: Dear friends, St John the Almsgiver lost his wife and his children. Grief could have closed his heart; instead it opened it to a whole city. As Patriarch of Alexandria he asked for a list of his masters, and when asked who they were, he said: the poor.

Proverbs says that whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and will be repaid in full (Proverbs 19:17). John believed it. He fed thousands, built hospitals, sheltered refugees. Tradition says that a costly blanket given to him was sold for the poor again and again.

Who are our masters? Let us look at the poor in our parish with respect, not pity. This week let us set aside a share for those in need and visit one person who suffers. Whatever we give, we lend to the Lord. Amen.

johnalmsgiver.prayer: Lord God, you made St John the Almsgiver a father to the poor. Through his prayers, open our hearts and hands to those in need, and let us serve them as our masters. Amen.

johnchrysostom.t: Archbishop of Constantinople, Doctor of the Church
word: Proclaim the message; be persistent whether the time is favorable or unfavorable; convince, rebuke, and encourage, with the utmost patience in teaching.
2 Timothy 4:2
life: John was born in Antioch around 347. After years as a monk he was ordained a priest and became the greatest preacher of his age; later generations called him Chrysostom, the golden-mouthed. In 398 he was made Archbishop of Constantinople.

He preached against the luxury of the rich and the neglect of the poor, reformed the clergy and cared for the sick. His frankness made powerful enemies, including the empress Eudoxia; he was deposed and exiled, and died in 407 on a forced march at Comana in Pontus. The Latin Church keeps his memorial on 13 September; the Eastern Churches remember him on 13 November.
lessons: Preach in season and out
He spoke the truth whether it pleased or not.
Honour Christ in the poor
He taught that we cannot honour Christ at the altar and ignore him in the street.
Gratitude in suffering
Tradition gives his last words as: glory to God for all things.
stories: Glory to God for all things
His early biographer Palladius records that, dying in exile, John gave thanks to God for everything.
quotes: Glory to God for all things.
St John Chrysostom's last words, as handed down by tradition
p

points: Be persistent whether the time is favourable or unfavourable (2 Timothy 4:2).
The Christ we honour in the Holy Qurbono waits for us in the poor.
Glory to God for all things: gratitude even in suffering.
homily: Dear friends, St John Chrysostom was called the golden-mouthed because his preaching moved thousands. But his words were not only beautiful; they were brave. Paul had told Timothy to proclaim the message whether the time is favourable or unfavourable (2 Timothy 4:2), and John did.

He told the rich of Constantinople that it is useless to honour Christ's body in church with silk vestments while leaving him naked and cold outside. He reformed the clergy and cared for the sick. For this he was exiled, and he died on the road.

Tradition says his last words were: glory to God for all things. Let us learn from him to honour Christ both at the altar and in the poor, to speak the truth with love, and to thank God even in hardship. Amen.

johnchrysostom.prayer: Lord God, you gave St John Chrysostom the gift of eloquence and the courage of truth. Through his prayers, make us honour Christ in the Holy Qurbono and in the poor, and give thanks to you for all things. Amen.

philipapostle.n: Mar Philipose Shleeha (St Philip the Apostle)
philipapostle.t: Apostle, who said: come and see
word: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
John 14:9
life: Philip was from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter. Jesus found him and said: follow me. Philip at once found Nathanael and told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about; when Nathanael doubted, Philip said: come and see (John 1:43–46).

Before the feeding of the five thousand Jesus tested Philip by asking where they could buy bread (John 6:5–7); Greeks who wanted to see Jesus came first to Philip (John 12:21); and at the Last Supper Philip asked: Lord, show us the Father (John 14:8). Tradition says he preached in Asia Minor and died at Hierapolis in Phrygia. The Latin Church keeps his feast with St James on 3 May; the Eastern Churches remember him on 14 November.
lessons: Come and see
Philip did not argue; he invited.
Honest questions
His questions led to some of Jesus' greatest answers.
Seeing the Father in Jesus
The face of God is shown to us in Christ.
stories: When Nathanael asked whether anything good could come from Nazareth, Philip simply said: come and see (John 1:46).

points: Philip's way of mission: an invitation, not an argument (John 1:46).
Our deepest longing is to see God.
In Jesus we see the Father (John 14:9).
homily: Dear friends, today we remember Mar Philipose Shleeha. When he met Jesus, he ran to his friend Nathanael. Nathanael was doubtful: can anything good come out of Nazareth? Philip did not argue. He said: come and see (John 1:46).

At the Last Supper Philip asked what every human heart asks: Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied. Jesus answered: have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:8–9).

We do not need to win arguments to share our faith. We need to invite: come and see, to a prayer meeting, to the Holy Qurbono, to a family rosary. And let us look more deeply at Jesus, for in him we see the Father. Amen.

philipapostle.prayer: Lord Jesus, you called Philip to follow you and showed him the Father. Through his prayers, help us to invite others to come and see, and to know the Father in you. Amen.

matthewapostle.n: Mar Mathai Shleeha (St Matthew the Apostle)
word: As Jesus was walking along, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth; and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
Matthew 9:9
life: Matthew, also called Levi, was a tax collector at Capernaum, working for the authorities and despised by his own people. Jesus saw him at the tax booth and said: follow me; and he got up and followed. That same day Jesus ate at his house with tax collectors and sinners, saying that he came to call not the righteous but sinners (Matthew 9:9–13).

The Church has from early times attributed to Matthew the first Gospel, which presents Jesus as the fulfilment of the Law and the prophets. Traditions differ on where he preached and died, naming Ethiopia or Persia. The Latin Church keeps his feast on 21 September; the Eastern Churches remember him on 16 November.
lessons: No one is beyond the call
Jesus called a despised tax collector.
Leave and follow
Matthew left his booth at once.
Mercy, not sacrifice
Jesus quoted Hosea to explain his table fellowship with sinners.
stories: Matthew celebrated his call with a meal for his fellow tax collectors, and Jesus sat among them (Matthew 9:10).

points: He saw a man everyone else had written off.
Two words changed a life; Matthew got up at once.
homily: Dear friends, today we remember Mar Mathai Shleeha. Matthew sat at the tax booth, a man his neighbours despised. Jesus passed by, looked at him and said two words: follow me. And he got up and followed him (Matthew 9:9).

That evening Matthew gave a feast for his friends, tax collectors and sinners, and Jesus sat with them. When the Pharisees complained, Jesus answered: I desire mercy, not sacrifice; I have come to call not the righteous but sinners (Matthew 9:13).
No one is too far from God to be called. Jesus still looks at each of us with love and says: follow me. Let us answer at once, and let our table, like Matthew's, be open to those others reject. Amen.

matthewapostle.prayer: Lord Jesus, you called Matthew from the tax booth to be your apostle and evangelist. Through his prayers, help us to answer your call at once and to show mercy to all. Amen.

clementfelicity.n: St Clement, Pope, and St Felicity
word: Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same purpose.
1 Corinthians 1:10
life: Clement was one of the first bishops of Rome, listed by St Irenaeus as the third successor of Peter. Around AD 96 he wrote a letter to the Church in Corinth, which was divided by quarrels, urging them to peace, humility and order. It is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament. A later tradition says that he was exiled to the Crimea and martyred by drowning with an anchor; this is regarded as legend.

Felicity was a Roman martyr buried on the Via Salaria. A later account, largely legendary, says she was a widow who encouraged her seven sons to die for Christ before she herself was martyred. Both are named in the ancient Roman Canon of the Mass.
lessons: Peacemakers in the Church
Clement wrote to heal divisions; we too can heal quarrels.
Faith handed down in families
Felicity is remembered as a mother who strengthened her children's faith.
The Church of the first centuries
Their memory links us with the earliest Christians.
stories: Clement's letter to the Corinthians, still preserved, asks the community to put away jealousy and live in harmony.
A later legend says Clement was thrown into the sea with an anchor tied to him; he is often shown with an anchor.

points: Paul and Clement both wrote to Corinth begging for unity (1 Corinthians 1:10).
A good tree bears good fruit: peace is the fruit of humility.
Felicity's story honours parents who form their children in faith.
homily: Dear friends, today we remember two early martyrs of Rome. Clement, one of the first bishops of Rome, wrote around the year 96 to the Christians of Corinth, who were quarrelling and dividing. Like Paul before him, he begged them to be united in the same mind (1 Corinthians 1:10), to put away jealousy and to live humbly.

Felicity is honoured as a Roman martyr; a later account, largely legendary, remembers her as a mother who strengthened her sons to remain faithful. Whatever the details, the Church has prayed her name in the Mass for many centuries.

Two lessons for us: be peacemakers in the Church and in the family, and pass on the faith to your children. A good tree bears good fruit. Let our parishes be known for harmony, and our homes for faith. Amen.

clementfelicity.prayer: Lord God, you gave your Church St Clement as a shepherd of peace and St Felicity as a mother of faith. Through their prayers, keep us united in your Church and faithful in our families. Amen.

ambrose.t: Bishop of Milan, Doctor of the Church
word: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
Psalm 119:105
life: Ambrose was born around 339 at Trier, in a Roman Christian family. He studied law and rhetoric and became governor of the province whose capital was Milan, then one of the great cities of the empire.

In 374 the bishop of Milan died, and the election of a successor threatened to end in riot between Catholics and Arians. Ambrose went to the church to keep order; the people began to cry out for him as bishop. He was still only a catechumen. Within about a week he was baptised, ordained and consecrated bishop.

He gave his wealth to the poor, studied the Scriptures and the Greek Fathers, and became a great preacher and writer. He introduced hymn singing to the people of Milan, and some of his hymns are still sung. He defended the faith of Nicaea and the freedom of the Church before emperors, and after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390 he required the emperor Theodosius to do public penance before receiving Communion.

His preaching helped to bring the young professor Augustine to faith, and Ambrose baptised him at the Easter Vigil of 387. He died on 4 April 397. He is one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church.
lessons: Called unexpectedly
God called Ambrose through the voice of the people when he least expected it.
Truth before power
He corrected even the emperor, with courage and respect.
The Word nourishes
He soaked his preaching in Scripture and the Fathers.
Prayer in song
His hymns taught the faith to ordinary people.
stories: In 374, while Ambrose was trying to calm a divided crowd in the cathedral of Milan, the people began to call for him as bishop, though he was not yet baptised. He tried to avoid the office but accepted it as God's will.

After soldiers of Theodosius massacred thousands at Thessalonica in 390, Ambrose wrote to the emperor that he could not offer the Eucharist in his presence until he repented. Theodosius did public penance.
Augustine writes in his Confessions that he came to Milan, heard Ambrose preach, and was slowly won over to the faith. Ambrose baptised him in 387.
quotes: Where Peter is, there is the Church.
St Ambrose, Commentary on Psalm 40, in substance
p
ambrose.prayer: Lord God, you made St Ambrose a teacher of the faith and a model of apostolic courage; raise up in your Church shepherds after your own heart, who will guide your people with wisdom and strength. Amen.

points: God called a governor to be a bishop; He can call us in surprising ways.
Ambrose corrected the emperor but welcomed his repentance.
His preaching won Augustine; our words and lives can lead others.
homily: Dear friends, St Ambrose was a successful Roman governor when the people of Milan, gathered to elect a bishop, began to shout: Ambrose, bishop! He was not even baptised. Yet he recognised in that cry the call of God, and within a week he was baptised and consecrated.
He gave away his wealth and threw himself into study and prayer. His sermons were full of Scripture, and he taught the people to sing hymns. He became one of the great teachers of the Church.

Ambrose had courage. When the emperor Theodosius ordered a massacre at Thessalonica, Ambrose told him he must do penance before receiving Communion. The emperor humbled himself and repented. Ambrose spoke the truth with love, and he rejoiced at the emperor's conversion.

His greatest fruit was a restless young man named Augustine, who came to Milan, listened to Ambrose and was baptised by him. Let us ask St Ambrose to help us speak the truth with courage and love, and to lead others to Christ by our words and lives. Amen.

juandiego.t: Indigenous layman of Mexico, messenger of Our Lady of Guadalupe
word: he has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly;
Luke 1:52
life: Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin was born around 1474 among the Chichimeca people near present-day Mexico City. He was baptised as an adult by Franciscan missionaries in the 1520s, together with his wife, and walked long distances to attend Mass and catechism.

In December 1531, according to the tradition of the Church in Mexico, the Virgin Mary appeared to him on the hill of Tepeyac, speaking to him in his own Nahuatl language and asking that a church be built there. The bishop, Fray Juan de Zumárraga, asked for a sign.

On 12 December Mary told Juan Diego to gather flowers on the hilltop, though it was winter. He carried them in his tilma, a cloak of cactus fibre, to the bishop. When he opened it, the flowers fell out and an image of Our Lady was seen on the cloth. That tilma is venerated today in the Basilica of Guadalupe.

Juan Diego spent the rest of his life near the chapel built at Tepeyac, caring for it and telling pilgrims of the Virgin's message. He died in 1548. Pope John Paul II canonised him in Mexico City in 2002.
lessons: God chooses the humble
Mary sent a poor indigenous man to the bishop.
Faith in one's own culture
Mary spoke his language and wore the dress of his people.
Perseverance
Juan Diego returned to the bishop again and again.
Care for the sick
He hurried to find a priest for his dying uncle.
stories: According to the tradition, Mary told Juan Diego to gather flowers from the frozen hilltop and carry them to the bishop in his tilma. When he opened it, the image of the Virgin appeared on the cloth.
Am I not here, who am your mother?

When Juan Diego took another road to avoid Mary because his uncle was dying, she met him and comforted him with words remembered in the Nican Mopohua account: am I not here, who am your mother? His uncle was healed.
juandiego.prayer: Lord, through St Juan Diego you showed your love for the humble and the poor; grant that, following his example, we may welcome Mary's message and bring Christ to every people. Amen.

points: God chose a humble layman to speak to the bishop.
Juan Diego kept going even when he was not believed.
homily: Dear friends, St Juan Diego was a poor indigenous man in Mexico, baptised as an adult, who walked many miles to attend Mass. In 1531, according to the tradition of the Church in Mexico, the Virgin Mary appeared to him on the hill of Tepeyac and sent him to the bishop with a message.
Notice whom Mary chose: not a rich Spaniard or a learned priest, but a humble layman of a conquered people. As Mary sang in the Magnificat, God lifts up the lowly (Luke 1:52).

Mary spoke to him in his own language and appeared with the features and dress of his people. The Gospel is not foreign to any culture. Christ wants to be at home in every people, in Mexico, in India and everywhere.

Juan Diego was not believed at first, but he persevered, and his tilma with the image of Our Lady became a sign for millions. Let us ask him to help us carry God's message humbly and faithfully, even when we are not believed. Amen.

word: A great portent appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.
Revelation 12:1
life: In December 1531, ten years after the fall of the Aztec capital, the Virgin Mary appeared, according to the tradition of the Church in Mexico, to the indigenous layman Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac. She asked that a church be built there, where she would show her love and compassion to all who called on her.

As a sign for the bishop, her image appeared on Juan Diego's tilma. It shows a young woman with features of the native peoples, standing on the moon, clothed with the sun, with her hands joined in prayer and a sash that, in the culture of the time, indicated a woman with child.

In the years that followed, very many indigenous people received Baptism. The image is venerated in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City, one of the most visited Marian shrines in the world. Popes have honoured Our Lady of Guadalupe as Patroness of the Americas and of the unborn.
lessons: A mother for every people
Mary came as one of the people she visited.
Christ at the centre
The image shows Mary with child, bearing Christ.
Hope after defeat
She came to a wounded people.
stories: According to the tradition, when Juan Diego opened his cloak before Bishop Zumárraga, the flowers fell to the floor and the image of the Virgin was seen on the cloth. The tilma is displayed in the Basilica of Guadalupe.
Because the image shows Mary with child, she is invoked today as protector of unborn life.
guadalupe.prayer: God of mercy, you placed your people under the special protection of the Mother of your Son; through the intercession of Our Lady of Guadalupe, may we seek your justice and peace and defend every human life. Amen.

points: A woman clothed with the sun
The sash shows she is with child.
She came to the poor and defeated.
homily: Dear friends, today we honour Our Lady of Guadalupe. In 1531, according to the tradition, Mary appeared to Juan Diego in Mexico and left her image on his cloak. The image recalls the vision of Revelation: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet (Revelation 12:1).
In the image Mary wears a sash that, in the culture of that time, showed that a woman was expecting a child. Mary comes carrying Christ. All true devotion to Mary leads to her Son.
She came to a people who had just been conquered and humiliated. She spoke their language and looked like them. She brought them not weapons but consolation, and through her millions came to Christ.

Today let us pray to Our Lady of Guadalupe for all mothers, especially those expecting a child in difficulty, for the protection of unborn life, and for all peoples who suffer. May she bring Christ to them as she did in Mexico. Amen.

word: You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.
Matthew 5:14
life: Lucy was a young Christian of Syracuse in Sicily who died as a martyr, probably during the persecution of Diocletian around 304. Her veneration is very ancient: an inscription from Syracuse of the late fourth or early fifth century mentions her feast, and her name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

Her later Acts, which historians regard as largely legendary, tell that she consecrated her virginity to God, gave her dowry to the poor, and was denounced by a disappointed suitor. Condemned, she could not be moved by force, and was finally killed with a sword.

Her name comes from the Latin word for light. Her feast falls in the darkest days of the northern year, and in many countries it is kept with lights and processions. Because of a later legend about her eyes, she is invoked as patron of those with eye disease.
lessons: A light in the darkness
Her name and feast speak of Christ the Light.
Generosity to the poor
She gave her wealth away.
Firm in faith
No force could move her from Christ.
stories: The Acts tell that guards tried to drag Lucy away with ropes and even oxen, but could not move her.
A medieval legend says that her eyes were taken out and restored by God; she is often pictured holding two eyes on a dish, and is invoked by those with eye trouble.
lucy.prayer: Lord, may the prayers of St Lucy, virgin and martyr, give us courage, so that we may be lights in the world and come to see your glory. Amen.

points: Lucy reminds us of Christ the Light.
homily: Dear friends, St Lucy was a young Christian martyr of Sicily in the great persecution around the year 304. Her name means light, and her feast comes in the darkest days of the northern year, in the middle of Advent.

We know little for certain about her life, but her memory was honoured very early; her name is in the Roman Canon. Later stories tell that she gave her dowry to the poor and that no force could move her from her faith. Whatever the details, the heart is clear: she preferred Christ to everything.
Jesus said: you are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14). Lucy's light was not her own; it was the light of Christ shining through her courage and generosity.

In this Advent season, let us be lights: by generosity to the poor, by firmness in faith, by kindness in dark situations. And let us pray for all who suffer from eye disease, and for all who live in spiritual darkness. Amen.

johncross.t: Carmelite priest, mystic, Doctor of the Church
word: More than that, I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.
Philippians 3:8
life: Juan de Yepes was born in 1542 at Fontiveros in Spain, into a poor family; his father died when he was a child. He worked in a hospital while studying with the Jesuits, and in 1563 he entered the Carmelite Order. He studied at Salamanca and was ordained priest in 1567.

That year he met St Teresa of Ávila, who was reforming the Carmelite nuns, and she asked him to help her begin the same reform among the friars. He became one of the first Discalced Carmelites, taking the name John of the Cross.

The reform met strong opposition. In 1577 John was taken by force and imprisoned for about nine months in a tiny cell in Toledo, where he was beaten and humiliated. There, in darkness, he composed poems of love for God. In 1578 he escaped.

He served as superior and spiritual director and wrote great works on prayer: The Ascent of Mount Carmel, The Dark Night, The Spiritual Canticle and The Living Flame of Love. He died at Úbeda on 14 December 1591. He was canonised in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.
lessons: God alone
Let go of everything that is not God, in order to find God.
The dark night
Dryness and suffering can be God's purification.
Love without measure
In the evening of life we will be judged on love.
stories: In 1577 John was held in a narrow cell in the Carmelite priory at Toledo for about nine months. There he composed much of the Spiritual Canticle. He escaped by night in 1578.
St Teresa of Ávila affectionately called the small John her little Seneca, praising his wisdom.
quotes: In the evening of life, we will be examined on love.
St John of the Cross, Sayings of Light and Love, in substance
p
johncross.prayer: O God, you gave St John of the Cross a great love of the Cross and of self-denial; grant that we may follow his example and come to see your glory for ever. Amen.

points: Like St Paul, John counted all things loss for Christ.
God purifies us when we feel nothing.
At the end, only love remains.
homily: Dear friends, St John of the Cross was a small Carmelite friar with a very big heart. With St Teresa of Ávila he worked to renew the Carmelite Order. For this he was imprisoned by his own brothers, locked in a dark cell, beaten and humiliated.

In that darkness he wrote some of the most beautiful love poems ever written, poems of the soul's love for God. Like St Paul, he regarded everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8).

John teaches about the dark night: times when prayer is dry and God seems absent. He says that these times are not punishment, but God's way of purifying our love, so that we love Him for Himself and not for His gifts.
He also said that in the evening of life we will be examined on love. If you are going through a dark night, do not give up. Keep praying, keep loving. God is closer than you think. Amen.

word: While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Acts 7:59
life: Stephen was one of the seven men chosen by the community in Jerusalem, with the laying on of hands by the apostles, to serve at the daily distribution of food, so that the widows of the Greek-speaking Christians would not be neglected (Acts 6:1–6). The Church sees in the Seven the beginning of the diaconate.

Luke describes Stephen as full of faith and the Holy Spirit, full of grace and power, working great wonders and signs. His opponents could not withstand the wisdom with which he spoke, and they brought him before the Council on false charges (Acts 6:8–15).

In a long speech Stephen retold the history of Israel and accused his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit as their ancestors had done. Enraged, they dragged him out of the city and stoned him. He saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and he died praying for his killers (Acts 7). A young man named Saul, the future apostle Paul, approved of his death.
lessons: Service and witness
Holiness began in serving widows at table.
Full of the Spirit
His wisdom came from the Spirit.
Forgiveness
He died forgiving, like Jesus.
stories: As the stones fell, Stephen gazed into heaven and said that he saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55–56).
The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who approved of the killing (Acts 7:58; 8:1). Saul later became Paul the apostle.
stephenmartyr.prayer: Grant, Lord, that we may imitate St Stephen, who prayed for those who persecuted him, and learn to love even our enemies. Amen.

points: From the table to the altar of martyrdom
Faithful service prepared Stephen for witness.
He saw Jesus standing to receive him.
His prayer bore fruit in Paul.
homily: Dear friends, St Stephen is the first martyr of the Church. Before he gave his life, he served tables, making sure the poor widows received their food. Holiness began for him in practical service.
He was full of grace and of the Holy Spirit, and no one could withstand his wisdom. When he was brought before the Council, his face shone like an angel's.

As they stoned him, he looked up and saw heaven opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. He prayed: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:59), and then: Lord, do not hold this sin against them.
Among those watching was Saul, who would become St Paul. Stephen's forgiveness bore fruit. Let us ask St Stephen for the grace to serve humbly, to bear witness bravely, and to forgive fully. Amen.

word: God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them.
1 John 4:16
life: John, son of Zebedee and brother of James, was a fisherman of Galilee called by Jesus with his brother from their boat (Mark 1:19–20). Jesus called the two brothers Boanerges, sons of thunder (Mark 3:17). With Peter and James he witnessed the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane.

The Church has traditionally identified him with the disciple whom Jesus loved, who leaned on Jesus' breast at the Last Supper, stood at the foot of the Cross, and received Mary as his mother (John 19:26–27). On Easter morning he ran to the tomb with Peter, saw and believed (John 20:2–8).

Tradition attributes to him the Fourth Gospel, three letters and the Book of Revelation, and says that he lived to old age at Ephesus. His Gospel and letters are full of the themes of light, life, truth and above all love.
lessons: Close to the heart of Jesus
Prayer as resting on His breast.
Faithful at the Cross
John did not run away.
Taking Mary home
Every disciple receives Mary as mother.
God is love
The heart of his message.
stories: At the foot of the Cross

Jesus, seeing His mother and the disciple whom He loved, said to her: Woman, here is your son; and to the disciple: Here is your mother. And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home (John 19:26–27).

St Jerome records that when John was very old at Ephesus, he was carried to the assembly and repeated only: little children, love one another; when asked why, he said: it is the Lord's command, and if this alone is done, it is enough.
johnapostle.prayer: God our Father, through the apostle John you revealed the mysteries of your Word; grant that we may understand what he taught and live in the love he proclaimed. Amen.

points: Every Christian can lean on the heart of Jesus.
At the Cross John received Mary.
homily: Dear friends, St John was a young fisherman whom Jesus called the son of thunder, but he became the apostle of love. The Gospel calls him the disciple whom Jesus loved. At the Last Supper he leaned on Jesus' breast.

When the other disciples fled, John stood at the foot of the Cross with Mary. Jesus gave them to each other: here is your son, here is your mother. And from that hour John took her into his home (John 19:27).
His letters sum up the Gospel in three words: God is love (1 John 4:16). Tradition says that in old age he repeated only: little children, love one another.
In this Christmas season, let us learn from John to rest on the heart of Jesus in prayer, to take Mary into our homes, and to love one another, because this is the Lord's command. Amen.

word: A voice was heard in Ramah, wailing and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be consoled, because they are no more.
Matthew 2:18
life: When the Magi did not return to tell him where the newborn King of the Jews was, King Herod, fearing for his throne, ordered the killing of all the boys in Bethlehem and its surroundings who were two years old or under (Matthew 2:16).
