Joseph, warned in a dream, had already fled with the child and His mother to Egypt. Matthew sees in the mothers' grief the fulfilment of Jeremiah's words about Rachel weeping for her children.

From early centuries the Church has honoured these children as martyrs, because they died in place of Christ. Herod's cruelty is well known from history; Bethlehem was a small town, and the number of children killed may have been small, but each one was precious to God. In the Syro-Malabar Church the day is kept as Holy Childhood Day.
lessons: Every child is precious
God cares for each little one.
Protect the innocent
We are called to be Josephs, not Herods.
God hears the cry
Rachel's tears are not ignored.
stories: An angel told Joseph in a dream to take the child and His mother and flee to Egypt, and he left that very night (Matthew 2:13–14).
The historian Josephus describes Herod as a ruler who killed even members of his own family to protect his throne, which fits Matthew's account.
holyinnocents.prayer: O God, the Holy Innocents bore witness to you not by speaking but by dying; grant that we may protect every child and bear witness to you by our lives. Amen.

points: God hears the grief of parents.
homily: Dear friends, three days after Christmas we remember the little boys of Bethlehem killed by Herod. They could not speak, but the Church honours them as martyrs, because they died in place of Christ.
Matthew hears in the mothers' cry the voice of Rachel weeping for her children (Matthew 2:18). God hears that cry. Let us pray today for parents who have lost children.
Herod's fear made him cruel. There are still Herods: those who sacrifice children to protect their power or comfort. Children today suffer from abortion, abuse, hunger, war and exploitation.
Let us be like Joseph, who rose in the night to protect the child. Let us make our homes and parishes safe for children, and support those who care for children in need. Amen.

word: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
Matthew 16:18
life: Sylvester was Bishop of Rome from 314 to 335, in the years just after the emperor Constantine granted freedom to Christians in 313. After centuries of persecution, the Church could worship openly and build churches.

During his pontificate the great basilicas of Rome began to rise, including the Lateran and the first basilica of St Peter. In 325 the Council of Nicaea defined that the Son is of one substance with the Father; Sylvester was represented there by his legates.

Later legends said that Sylvester baptised Constantine and received from him rule over the West, but these stories are not historical: Constantine was baptised near the end of his life in 337. Sylvester died on 31 December 335 and was among the first non-martyrs honoured as saints in Rome.
lessons: Faithful in peace
Holiness is needed in times of freedom too.
Unity of faith
The Council of Nicaea defended the true faith.
Truth over legend
We honour the saints truthfully.
stories: In 325 more than two hundred bishops met at Nicaea and professed that the Son is true God from true God. Sylvester sent priests to represent him.
A medieval legend says that Sylvester healed and baptised Constantine; in fact Constantine was baptised in 337, shortly before his death.
sylvester.prayer: Lord, help your people through the intercession of Pope St Sylvester, and as we end this year, keep us faithful to the faith of the apostles. Amen.

points: The Church enters a time of freedom.
homily: Dear friends, on the last day of the year we remember Pope St Sylvester. He led the Church in Rome just after the long persecutions ended, when Christians could finally worship freely.

Freedom brought new challenges: comfort, worldliness, and the temptation to rely on power. In those years the Council of Nicaea professed the faith we still pray in the Creed: Jesus Christ is true God from true God, of one substance with the Father.

Later legends made Sylvester into a wonder-worker who baptised the emperor, but the truth is simpler: he was a faithful shepherd in a time of change. Peter's faith, the rock on which Christ builds His Church (Matthew 16:18), was kept firm.
As we end this year, let us thank God for the faith handed down to us, and ask for the grace to remain faithful in times of ease as well as hardship. Amen.

johndamascene.t: Monk, theologian and hymn writer, Doctor of the Church
word: And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father's only son, full of grace and truth.
John 1:14
life: John was born around 675 in Damascus into a Christian family that served in the financial administration of the Muslim caliphs. He received a fine education and himself held office at the court.
Around the beginning of the eighth century he left public life and became a monk at the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, where he was ordained a priest. There he prayed, studied and wrote.

When the Byzantine emperor Leo III began to forbid and destroy holy images, John wrote three famous defences of the icons. He argued that since the invisible God became visible in Christ, who took flesh, we may make images of Christ and the saints, honouring them without worshipping them. His great work The Fount of Knowledge sums up the faith of the Greek Fathers, and many of his hymns are still sung in the Eastern Churches.
He died around 749 at Mar Saba. Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1890.
lessons: Because God became visible
The Incarnation is the foundation of sacred images.
Honour, not worship
We venerate images; we adore God alone.
Faith that sings
Theology can become hymns.
stories: From the safety of the monastery, outside the emperor's control, John wrote that he did not worship matter, but the Creator of matter who became matter for his sake.
johndamascene.prayer: Lord, through the prayers of St John of Damascus, may the true faith he taught be our light, and may we always honour the mystery of your Word made flesh. Amen.

points: Images help us remember and pray.
homily: Dear friends, St John of Damascus was a Christian who held office in the court of the caliphs, and then left everything to become a monk near Jerusalem.

In his time, an emperor ordered holy images to be destroyed. John defended them with a simple argument: in Christ the invisible God became visible. Because the Word became flesh (John 1:14), we can paint His face. When we honour an icon, our honour goes to the person it shows.
Our Church loves the holy images, the Cross and the vestments, because they help us remember the mysteries of salvation. But we never worship images; we adore God alone.

John also wrote hymns still sung in the East. His theology was prayer. During this fast, let us look at an icon of Christ or of Mary and pray before it, giving thanks that God has shown us His face. Amen.

marsaba.t: Monk and founder of monasteries in the Judean desert
word: Be still, and know that I am God!
Psalm 46:10
life: Sabbas was born in 439 in Cappadocia, in present-day Turkey. As a boy he entered a monastery, and at about eighteen he went to Jerusalem and the desert of Judea, where he lived under the guidance of great monks such as St Euthymius.

After years of solitude in a cave above the Kidron valley, disciples gathered around him, and in 483 he founded the Great Lavra, a community of hermits who lived alone during the week and gathered for worship. The monastery, known as Mar Saba, still exists and is one of the oldest inhabited monasteries in the world.

Sabbas founded several other monasteries, was appointed leader of the hermits of Palestine, and travelled to Constantinople to defend the faith of the Council of Chalcedon and to intercede for the people. He died in 532, aged about ninety-three.
lessons: Silence and prayer
The desert teaches us to listen to God.
Community and solitude
Both are needed in the spiritual life.
Serving the Church
Even a hermit served the wider Church.
stories: The monastery founded by Sabbas in 483 clings to the cliffs of the Kidron valley and has housed monks almost continuously for over fifteen centuries.
marsaba.prayer: Lord, through the prayers of Mar Saba, teach us silence and prayer, and keep us faithful to your Church. Amen.

points: Silence is the school of prayer.
Prayer bears fruit for the Church.
homily: Dear friends, Mar Saba left his home as a youth and went to the desert of Judea to seek God in silence. The psalm says: be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10).

Many came to learn from him, and he founded the Great Lavra, where monks lived alone during the week and gathered on Saturdays and Sundays for the Holy Qurbono. That monastery still stands today, after fifteen centuries.
Mar Saba was not cut off from the Church. He travelled to the emperor to defend the true faith and to help his people. Prayer made him strong in service.
During this fast, let us find a little desert each day: ten minutes of silence, without phone or noise, to be still before God. Amen.

behnamsarah.n: Mar Behnam, his sister Sarah and the Forty Martyrs
behnamsarah.t: Martyrs honoured in the Syriac tradition
word: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
Romans 8:35
life: Mar Behnam and his sister Sarah are greatly honoured in the Syriac Churches, especially in northern Iraq, where the monastery of Mar Behnam near Mosul has been a place of pilgrimage for centuries.

According to the traditional account, Behnam and Sarah were children of a Persian ruler in the fourth century. Behnam came to faith through the holy monk Mar Mattai; Sarah was healed and baptised; and when their father learned that they had become Christians, he had them put to death together with forty companions. Later the father repented. Historians consider much of this account legendary, but it carries the memory of real martyrs of the Persian persecutions.
The monastery of Mar Behnam was damaged by militants in 2014–2015 and has since been restored, a sign of the endurance of Christians in the lands of their ancient faith.
lessons: Nothing separates us from Christ
Faith stronger than family pressure.
Brother and sister together
Faith shared in a family.
The suffering Church today
Christians of Iraq and the Middle East.
stories: The martyrdom of Behnam and Sarah
The traditional account tells that their father, angered by their conversion, had them killed with forty companions, and later repented and built a shrine in their memory.
After the damage of 2014–2015, the monastery of Mar Behnam near Mosul was restored and reopened for worship.
behnamsarah.prayer: Lord, through the prayers of Mar Behnam, his sister Sarah and the Forty Martyrs, strengthen Christians who suffer for their faith, especially in the lands of the East. Amen.

points: The Church of the East still suffers.
homily: Dear friends, today the Syriac tradition remembers Mar Behnam, his sister Sarah and forty companions. The traditional story, partly legendary, tells that they became Christians and were killed by their own father, a pagan ruler, who later repented.
St Paul asks: who will separate us from the love of Christ? Hardship, persecution, sword? (Romans 8:35). The martyrs answer with their lives: nothing.

Their monastery near Mosul has seen centuries of pilgrims and, in our own time, war and destruction. It was damaged by militants and then restored. Christians in Iraq and Syria still carry the cross of persecution.
Let us pray today for the Christians of the Middle East, our brothers and sisters in the Syriac tradition, and let us not be ashamed of our faith, which they keep at such cost. Amen.

rabbula.t: Bishop, reformer, friend of the poor
word: Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and will be repaid in full.
Proverbs 19:17
life: Rabbula was born in the late fourth century near Chalcis in Syria, into a wealthy family; his father was a pagan priest and his mother a Christian. After his conversion he gave away his property, freed his slaves and lived as a monk.

In 411 he became bishop of Edessa, the great centre of Syriac Christianity, and served until his death in 435 or 436. He was known for a strict and simple life, for reforming the clergy and monasteries, and especially for his care of the poor and the sick: he organised hospitals and relief for the needy.

He took part in the theological controversies of his time and worked for the faith of the Council of Ephesus (431), which proclaimed Mary Mother of God. He is honoured in the Syriac Churches as a holy bishop.
lessons: Wealth given away
Conversion changed how he used his money.
Care for the sick
A bishop who built hospitals.
Faithful teaching
Defending the Mother of God.
stories: Early Syriac accounts describe Rabbula organising care for the sick and poor of Edessa, including hospitals for men and women.
rabbula.prayer: Lord, through the prayers of Mar Rabbula, make us generous to the poor and faithful to the true faith. Amen.

points: He gave away wealth and freed slaves.
homily: Dear friends, Mar Rabbula was a rich man from Syria whose conversion changed everything. He gave away his property, freed his slaves and became a monk.
As bishop of Edessa he organised care for the poor and the sick, building hospitals. The Proverbs say: whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord (Proverbs 19:17).
He also worked to reform the clergy and monasteries, beginning with his own simple life, and he defended the faith that Mary is Mother of God.
During this Christmas fast, let us lend to the Lord by helping the poor and the sick. And let us ask Mar Rabbula to help our Church be holy and generous. Amen.

davidking.t: Shepherd of Bethlehem, ancestor of the Messiah
word: The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not want.
Psalm 23:1
life: David, the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, was a shepherd boy when the prophet Samuel anointed him as future king (1 Samuel 16). As a youth he defeated the Philistine Goliath, trusting in the Lord (1 Samuel 17).

After years as a fugitive from King Saul, he became king of Judah and then of all Israel, made Jerusalem his capital and brought the Ark of the Covenant there with dancing and joy (2 Samuel 6). God promised him through the prophet Nathan that his house and kingdom would endure for ever (2 Samuel 7).

David also sinned gravely with Bathsheba and against her husband Uriah. When Nathan confronted him, he repented (2 Samuel 12), and Psalm 51 is the Church's great prayer of repentance. Many psalms are attributed to him. Jesus, born in Bethlehem, is called the Son of David, and in Him God's promise is fulfilled.
lessons: God looks at the heart
The youngest shepherd was chosen.
Trust in battle
The Lord saves, not sword and spear.
Repentance
A great sinner became a great penitent.
Praying the psalms
David's prayers are ours.
stories: The young shepherd faced the giant with a sling and five stones, saying that the Lord does not save by sword and spear (1 Samuel 17:47).
The prophet Nathan told David a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man's lamb; when David was angry, Nathan said: you are the man. David repented (2 Samuel 12:7, 13).
davidking.prayer: Lord God, who promised David a kingdom without end and fulfilled your promise in Jesus Christ, give us David's trust and repentant heart, and teach us to pray with his psalms. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, three days after Yaldo our Church remembers David, the shepherd of Bethlehem. God sent Samuel to anoint a king among Jesse's sons, and chose the youngest, who was with the sheep. The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

David trusted God against Goliath, and became a great king. Yet he also fell into terrible sin. When the prophet Nathan said to him: you are the man, David did not make excuses; he repented. Psalm 51 is the prayer of that repentance.
God promised David a kingdom without end. That promise is fulfilled in Jesus, born in David's town of Bethlehem, the true Good Shepherd and eternal King.
Let us pray David's psalms: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want (Psalm 23:1), and Have mercy on me, O God (Psalm 51). They teach us to trust and to repent. Amen.

basilgregory.n: Sts Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen
basilgregory.t: Bishops and Doctors of the Church
word: But speaking the truth in love, we must grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ,
Ephesians 4:15
life: Basil and Gregory were both born around 329 or 330 in Cappadocia, in present-day Turkey. Basil came from a family of saints: his grandmother Macrina, his parents, his sister Macrina and his brothers Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste are all honoured as saints. Gregory was the son of the bishop of Nazianzus, also named Gregory, and his mother Nonna. The two young men met as students at Athens and became lifelong friends.

After his studies Basil was baptised, visited the monks of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia, and began a life of prayer and work in a community near his family estate at Annesi. Gregory joined him there for a time. Basil's rules for monks, written as answers to questions, shaped monastic life in the East for centuries. In 370 he became bishop of Caesarea. He resisted the pressure of the Arian emperor Valens, defended the divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and built outside the city a great centre of care for the poor, the sick, travellers and lepers.

Gregory, a gentle and sensitive man who loved solitude, was ordained priest by his father almost against his will. In 379 he was called to Constantinople, where the Catholic faith had few followers. In a small chapel he named Anastasia, Resurrection, he preached the five Theological Orations on the Holy Trinity, and the Eastern tradition has called him the Theologian ever since. He presided for a time over the Council of Constantinople in 381, but resigned for the sake of peace and returned home to pray and write poetry.

Basil died on 1 January 379, according to the traditional date, and Gregory around 390. Their writings, together with those of Gregory of Nyssa, helped the Church to express the faith in the Trinity that we profess in the Creed. A eucharistic liturgy bears Basil's name, and Basil and Gregory are honoured among the great Doctors of the Church in East and West. The Roman calendar keeps their feast together because of their friendship.
lessons: Friendship in Christ
Their friendship helped both of them to grow in holiness.
Faith that thinks
They used their learning to serve the truth of the Trinity.
Love for the poor
Basil's care for the sick and the hungry was part of his faith.
Humility in office
Gregory gave up a great see for the sake of peace.
stories: In his funeral oration for Basil, Gregory recalls their student days in Athens: they knew only two roads, one to the church and one to the schools, and they seemed to have one soul in two bodies.
Perhaps you have never met a bishop

Gregory records that when the prefect Modestus threatened Basil with confiscation, exile and death, Basil replied that he owned almost nothing, that every land was God's, and that death would only bring him sooner to God. When the prefect said that no one had ever spoken to him like that, Basil answered: perhaps you have never met a bishop.

Outside Caesarea Basil built a large complex with a hospital, a hostel for travellers and care for lepers. People called it the new city, and later the Basileiad. Gregory says Basil himself tended the sick.
quotes: The bread you keep belongs to the hungry; the coat in your wardrobe belongs to the naked.
St Basil the Great, Homily on the rich fool, in substance
p
We seemed to have one soul in two bodies.
St Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 43, in substance
p
basilgregory.prayer: O God, who were pleased to give light to your Church by the example and teaching of Sts Basil and Gregory, grant that in humility we may learn your truth and put it faithfully into practice with love. Amen.

points: They taught what we profess in the Creed.
Basil served the poor; Gregory gave up honour for peace.
homily: Dear friends, at the start of the new year the Church gives us two friends: Basil and Gregory. They met as students in Athens, and Gregory later wrote that they seemed to have one soul in two bodies. They knew only two roads: the road to the church and the road to the schools.

Their friendship was not only pleasant company; it was a shared journey towards God. They studied together, prayed together and lived for a time as monks together. A true friend helps us become better and holier. Let us thank God for such friends, and ask to be such a friend for others.

Both became bishops in a time of confusion, when many denied that the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly God. They defended the faith we profess every Sunday in the Creed. Yet their faith was not only in words. Basil built a city of mercy for the sick and the poor, and Gregory, when quarrels arose, gave up the great see of Constantinople for the sake of peace.

St Paul tells us to speak the truth in love and so grow up into Christ (Ephesians 4:15). That is the lesson of these two saints. Let us begin this year by holding firmly to the truth of our faith, by serving the poor, and by being faithful friends who help one another towards heaven. Amen.

josephvaz.t: Priest of Goa, Apostle of Sri Lanka
word: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.”
Isaiah 52:7
life: Joseph Vaz was born on 21 April 1651 in Goa, at Benaulim, into a Catholic Konkani family. He studied with the Jesuits and at the Dominican academy in Goa, and was ordained priest in 1676. He was known for his preaching and his care for the poor, and he made a personal act of consecration to Mary as her servant.

In 1681 he was sent to Kanara, around Mangalore, where Catholics were divided by a painful dispute between two Church jurisdictions. Joseph worked patiently for peace and for the good of the people. On his return to Goa he joined a new community of Goan priests following the way of life of St Philip Neri, the Oratory of the Holy Cross of Miracles, and became its superior.

He learned that the Catholics of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, had been left without priests: the Dutch rulers of the coast were Calvinists and forbade Catholic worship. In 1686 he left Goa secretly with a companion, travelling as a poor labourer, and reached Jaffna in 1687. He went from village to village at night, hearing confessions, celebrating Mass in hiding and strengthening the faithful. In 1692 he went to Kandy, the capital of the independent Sinhala kingdom, where he was imprisoned for some time as a suspected spy.

After his release he was allowed to work in the kingdom of Kandy. He cared for the sick during a smallpox epidemic, wrote and adapted prayers and catechisms in Sinhala and Tamil with his companions, and brought other priests from the Goan Oratory. He died at Kandy on 16 January 1711, having rebuilt the Catholic Church on the island. He was beatified in Colombo in 1995 by Pope John Paul II and canonised in Colombo on 14 January 2015 by Pope Francis.
lessons: Going where no one goes
He went to a people without priests at great risk.
Peacemaker
In Kanara he worked to heal division among Catholics.
The Gospel in the people's language
He used Sinhala and Tamil to teach the faith.
Service of the sick
He cared for the dying during an epidemic.
stories: To enter Ceylon unnoticed, Joseph travelled as a poor labourer and moved at night from one Catholic family to another, carrying what he needed for Mass.
In 1692 he was arrested in the kingdom of Kandy as a suspected Portuguese spy and held for a time. He used the period to learn Sinhala and to pray, and was later allowed to work freely.
Accounts preserved by the Oratorians tell that during a severe drought in Kandy Joseph prayed publicly and rain fell, and that after this the king allowed him to preach.
josephvaz.prayer: Lord our God, you made St Joseph Vaz a tireless messenger of the Gospel to the people of Sri Lanka; through his prayers, give us courage to bring your love to all who are without a shepherd. Amen.

points: He walked from village to village for Christ.
He went to Catholics left without priests.
A son of Goa became the apostle of a neighbouring land.
homily: Dear friends, St Joseph Vaz was a priest from Goa, a son of our own land. He could have stayed at home, respected and comfortable. But he heard that the Catholics of Ceylon had been left for years without priests, because the rulers there forbade Catholic worship.

So in 1686 he left secretly, dressed as a poor labourer, and crossed to the island. He walked from village to village at night, celebrating Mass in hiding, hearing confessions and baptising children. The prophet says: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace (Isaiah 52:7). Joseph's tired feet were beautiful in God's eyes.

He was arrested and imprisoned as a spy. He did not give up. He learned the people's language, cared for the sick in an epidemic, and gave them prayers and teaching in Sinhala and Tamil. When he died in 1711, the Church of Sri Lanka was alive again.

Joseph Vaz reminds us that India is not only a land that receives missionaries, but also one that sends them. Let us pray for all missionaries, especially those from India, and let us ask: who around me has no shepherd, and how can I bring Christ to them? Amen.

word: Jesus said to him, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
Matthew 19:21
life: Antony was born around 251 in a village of Middle Egypt, to Christian parents who owned land. When he was about eighteen or twenty his parents died, leaving him to care for his younger sister. Some months later he heard in church the Gospel words: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give to the poor. He took them as spoken to him. He gave away his land, entrusted his sister to a community of consecrated virgins, and began a life of prayer, work and fasting near his village.

Seeking greater solitude, he lived for a time in a tomb, and then for about twenty years alone in an abandoned fort in the desert near the Nile. There he struggled against temptations, which his biographer describes as attacks of demons. Around 305 he came out, calm and full of grace, and many people came to learn from him. Communities of hermits grew up around him, and he became known as the father of monks.

During the persecution of 311 he went to Alexandria to encourage the Christians in prison and in the mines, hoping to be a martyr himself, but he was not arrested. Afterwards he withdrew to the inner mountain near the Red Sea, where the Monastery of St Antony still stands. He came to Alexandria once more to support the faith of Nicaea against the Arians. He died in 356 at the age of about a hundred and five.

Soon after his death St Athanasius of Alexandria wrote his Life, which spread quickly in East and West and made the monastic life known everywhere. Antony is honoured in all the ancient Churches, including the East Syriac and West Syriac traditions, on 17 January. In the West he became a patron of farmers and animals.
lessons: Taking the Gospel literally
One reading of the Gospel changed his whole life.
The battle within
The spiritual life includes struggle against temptation.
Humility
Only humility escapes the snares of the enemy.
Prayer that serves
The hermit came out to support martyrs and the true faith.
stories: Athanasius tells that Antony, thinking about the first Christians who sold everything, entered church just as the Gospel of the rich young man was read, and went out at once to give away his land.
Augustine and the Life of Antony
In his Confessions, Augustine tells how a friend described the Life of Antony to him in Milan, and how that story moved him deeply in the days before his conversion.

St Jerome's Life of Paul tells that the aged Antony visited the older hermit Paul in the desert, and that a raven brought them a whole loaf instead of the usual half. Most scholars regard this story as legend.
quotes: I saw the snares of the enemy spread over all the earth, and I asked: who can escape them? And I heard a voice say: humility.
St Antony, Sayings of the Desert Fathers, in substance
p
antonyabbot.prayer: O God, who called St Antony the Abbot to serve you in the desert by a wonderful way of life, grant through his prayers that, denying ourselves, we may always love you above all things. Amen.

points: God still speaks through the Gospel read in the liturgy.
We too must fight against temptation.
Only the humble pass through the snares.
homily: Dear friends, St Antony was a young man of Egypt with land, money and a family to look after. One day in church he heard the Gospel: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me (Matthew 19:21). He believed that Christ was speaking to him, and he obeyed.

Do we listen like that when the Gospel is read in church? Antony did not treat it as an old story. He let it change his life. The same word is read to us every time we gather for the Eucharist. Let us ask for ears that hear and hearts that obey.

Antony went into the desert, and there he met not only silence but struggle. He fought temptations, which his biographer describes as attacks of demons. The desert showed him what is inside the human heart. We too have deserts: times of loneliness, temptation and dryness. Antony teaches us to hold on to prayer and to trust in Christ.

He once saw the snares of the enemy spread over the whole world and asked who could escape them. A voice answered: humility. Many came to him for advice, and he sent them away with peace. Let us ask St Antony to teach us to listen to the Gospel, to fight temptation with prayer, and to walk humbly with our God. Amen.

word: But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
1 Corinthians 1:27
life: Agnes was a young girl of Rome who was put to death for her faith, probably during the persecution of Diocletian in the early fourth century; some scholars place her death earlier, in the third century. St Ambrose, writing within a century of her death, says she was twelve years old. Her name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

We know about her from early witnesses: Ambrose, Pope Damasus, who wrote verses for her tomb, and the poet Prudentius. They agree that she was very young, that she refused to give up her consecration to Christ, and that she died bravely. They differ on the manner of her death: Ambrose speaks of the sword, Damasus of fire. Later Acts add dramatic details that historians regard as legendary.

She was buried on the Via Nomentana outside Rome. In the fourth century Constantina, a daughter of the emperor Constantine, built a basilica near her tomb, and the church of Sant'Agnese still stands there today. Her name recalls the Latin word for lamb, agnus, and the Greek word for pure, hagne.

On her feast two lambs are blessed in Rome, and their wool is later used to weave the pallium, the woollen band the Pope gives to metropolitan archbishops as a sign of communion with him and of the shepherd who carries the lost sheep.
lessons: Strength in weakness
God showed His power in a young girl.
Belonging to Christ
She would not give away a heart given to Him.
Courage of the young
Age is no limit to holiness.
Purity
She kept her love undivided for Christ.
stories: St Ambrose writes that Agnes was too young to be punished, yet ripe for victory, and that she went to her death more gladly than a bride to her wedding.
Each year on 21 January two lambs are blessed at Rome, and their wool is used to weave the pallia of archbishops.
The later Acts say that when Agnes was exposed to shame, her hair grew long to cover her, and that a man who tried to harm her was struck blind and then healed through her prayer.
quotes: She was too young to be punished, yet she was ripe for victory.
St Ambrose, On Virgins, in substance
p
agnes.prayer: Almighty, ever-living God, who choose what is weak in the world to confound the strong, grant that we, who celebrate the heavenly birthday of St Agnes, may follow her constancy in the faith. Amen.

points: A child put the powerful to shame.
Her lambs remind the Church of the Good Shepherd.
homily: Dear friends, St Agnes was only a girl, about twelve years old according to St Ambrose, when she died for Christ in Rome. The judges expected her to be afraid. Instead she stood firm. Ambrose wrote that she was too young to be punished, yet ripe for victory.

St Paul says: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27). The power of Rome was shamed by the courage of a child. Holiness does not depend on age, strength or position. It depends on love for Christ.

Agnes had given her heart to Christ, and she would not take it back, even when threatened with death. Today young people face other pressures: to follow the crowd, to give up purity, to hide their faith. Agnes shows that it is possible to belong wholly to Christ.

Every year on her feast two lambs are blessed in Rome, and their wool is used for the pallium of archbishops, a sign of the Good Shepherd. Let us pray for our young people, that they may be strong in faith like Agnes, and let us support them with our example and our prayer. Amen.

francisdesales.t: Bishop of Geneva, Doctor of the Church
word: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
Matthew 11:29
life: Francis de Sales was born on 21 August 1567 in the castle of Sales in Savoy, the eldest son of a noble family. His father wanted him to become a lawyer and a senator. He studied in Paris with the Jesuits and then law at Padua, where he received his doctorate. While in Paris he passed through a long and painful temptation to despair about his salvation; it ended when he prayed before an image of Our Lady and gave himself wholly to God's love.

Against his father's wishes he was ordained priest in 1593. The next year he volunteered for the Chablais, a region south of Lake Geneva that had become Calvinist. Doors were closed to him, so he wrote short leaflets explaining the Catholic faith and slipped them under doors. Over several years of patient preaching and kindness, very many people returned to the Catholic Church. Pope Pius XI later named him patron of writers and journalists.

In 1602 he became bishop of Geneva, living at Annecy because Geneva itself was closed to Catholics. He was a devoted pastor and a much sought spiritual director. His Introduction to the Devout Life, written for lay people, taught that holiness is possible in every state of life, in the home, the workplace and the court. His Treatise on the Love of God is a classic of spiritual theology.

With St Jane Frances de Chantal he founded in 1610 the Order of the Visitation. He died at Lyon on 28 December 1622. He was canonised in 1665 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1877. His feast is kept on 24 January, the day of his burial at Annecy.
lessons: Gentleness
He won hearts by kindness rather than force.
Holiness for everyone
Devotion belongs in every kind of life.
Creative witness
He used the written word to reach closed doors.
Trust in God's love
He came through despair by surrendering to God.
stories: In the Chablais, when people would not come to hear him, Francis wrote leaflets explaining the faith and slipped them under doors. They were later published as The Controversies.

As a student in Paris, Francis was tormented by fear that he was condemned. Kneeling before an image of Our Lady in the church of Saint-Étienne-des-Grès, he prayed the Memorare and offered himself to God whatever happened; the anguish left him.
Francis is remembered as gentle, but he said that he had a quick temper by nature and had worked for many years to master it.
quotes: A spoonful of honey attracts more flies than a barrel of vinegar.
St Francis de Sales, attributed saying, in substance
p
Nothing is so strong as gentleness, nothing so gentle as real strength.
St Francis de Sales, attributed, in substance
p
francisdesales.prayer: O God, who for the salvation of souls willed that St Francis de Sales become all things to all, graciously grant that, following his example, we may always show the gentleness of your love in the service of our neighbour. Amen.

points: Devotion is for mothers, workers and students too.
Love finds a way to share the faith.
homily: Dear friends, St Francis de Sales was a nobleman trained as a lawyer, but he gave up a brilliant career to become a priest. His first mission was to a region where people had left the Catholic Church. They closed their doors to him and even threatened him.

Francis did not give up. He wrote short leaflets explaining the faith and slipped them under the doors. Over the years, with patience, preaching and kindness, very many returned to the Church. Today he is the patron of writers and journalists. We too can use our words, and our phones, to spread truth and kindness.

He is famous for gentleness, but he said it did not come easily: he had to fight his own temper. Jesus says: learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29). Gentleness is not weakness; it is strength under the control of love.

Francis also taught that holiness is for everyone: the mother at home, the farmer in the field, the student at his desk. We do not need to leave our ordinary life to be holy; we need to live it with love for God. Let us ask St Francis de Sales to make us gentle, patient and holy in our everyday lives. Amen.

word: He asked, “Who are you, Lord?” The reply came, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
Acts 9:5
life: Saul was a Jew born in Tarsus in Cilicia, a Roman citizen by birth, brought up in Jerusalem and educated at the feet of the teacher Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). He was a Pharisee, zealous for the Law, and he violently persecuted the followers of Jesus. He approved of the stoning of Stephen and dragged believers to prison (Acts 7:58; 8:1–3; Galatians 1:13–14).

On the road to Damascus, where he was going to arrest Christians, a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? He asked: who are you, Lord? The answer came: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. The Acts of the Apostles tell this event three times (Acts 9, 22 and 26), and Paul himself speaks of it in his letters (Galatians 1:15–16; 1 Corinthians 15:8).

Blinded, he was led into Damascus, where for three days he neither ate nor drank. The Lord sent a disciple named Ananias, who laid hands on him; something like scales fell from his eyes, he regained his sight and was baptised (Acts 9:17–18). He began at once to proclaim Jesus as the Son of God. Paul later wrote that he went away to Arabia, returned to Damascus, and after three years went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter (Galatians 1:17–18).

The persecutor became the Apostle of the nations, the greatest missionary of the early Church, whose letters are part of the New Testament. Paul saw in his conversion a sign of God's mercy: if Christ could save him, the foremost of sinners, He could save anyone (1 Timothy 1:15–16). The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, kept in many places from 18 to 25 January, ends on this feast.
lessons: No one is beyond grace
The fiercest persecutor became the great apostle.
Christ and His Church are one
To persecute Christians was to persecute Christ.
Grace through the Church
Ananias and baptism were part of Paul's conversion.
A new beginning
Conversion is the start of a life of mission.
stories: A light from heaven flashed around Saul; he fell to the ground and heard the voice of Jesus asking why he persecuted Him (Acts 9:3–6).
Ananias was afraid to meet the persecutor, but the Lord told him that Saul was a chosen instrument. He went, called him brother Saul, and laid his hands on him (Acts 9:10–17).
Many paintings show Saul falling from a horse. The Acts do not mention a horse; this detail comes from later Christian art.
quotes: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.
St Paul, Galatians 2:19–20
conversionpaul.prayer: O God, who taught the whole world through the preaching of the blessed Apostle Paul, grant that we, who celebrate his conversion, may follow his example and become witnesses to your truth in the world. Amen.

points: The question that changed Saul's life.
No one is too far from God.
homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate a turning point in the history of the Church. Saul of Tarsus, a learned and zealous Pharisee, was on his way to Damascus to arrest Christians. Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him, and he heard a voice: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?

Saul asked: who are you, Lord? And the answer came: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (Acts 9:5). Notice: Jesus does not say, why do you persecute my followers, but why do you persecute me. Christ and His Church are one body. What we do to the least of His brothers and sisters, we do to Him.

Saul was blinded, and for three days he waited in darkness. Then the Lord sent Ananias, an ordinary disciple, who was afraid but obeyed. He laid hands on Saul and called him brother. Saul was baptised and began a new life. God uses people like Ananias to bring others to Christ.

The persecutor became the great Apostle of the nations. No one is too far from God's mercy, not even the person we find hardest to love. Let us pray today for the conversion of sinners, beginning with ourselves, and for the unity of all Christians, and let us ask each day like Paul: who are you, Lord, and what do you want me to do? Amen.

word: For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands;
2 Timothy 1:6
life: Timothy came from Lystra in Asia Minor. His father was a Greek and his mother Eunice a Jewish believer; Paul praises the sincere faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5). Paul took him as a companion on his second missionary journey, and Timothy became like a son to him (Philippians 2:19–22).

Timothy is named as co-sender of several of Paul's letters. Paul sent him to strengthen the churches of Thessalonica and Corinth (1 Thessalonians 3:2; 1 Corinthians 4:17) and left him in charge at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3). The two letters to Timothy in the New Testament give guidance for the pastoral care of a church. According to tradition, recorded by Eusebius, he was the first bishop of Ephesus; later accounts say he was killed there by a crowd for opposing a pagan festival.

Titus was a Greek, a Gentile convert. Paul took him to Jerusalem, and he was not required to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1–3). He was Paul's trusted envoy to the troubled church of Corinth, and his good news of their repentance brought Paul great comfort (2 Corinthians 7:6–7). Paul left him in Crete to put things in order and appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5), and later he went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10).

Tradition holds that Titus was the first bishop of Crete and died there in old age. Both men are examples of the second generation of Christian leaders, who received the faith from the apostles and handed it on faithfully. Their feast follows the feast of the Conversion of St Paul.
lessons: Faith handed on in the family
Timothy's faith came through his grandmother and mother.
Rekindle the gift
Grace received must be stirred up and used.
Young leaders
Paul trusted a young man with great responsibility.
Bringing peace
Titus helped reconcile a divided church.
stories: Paul reminds Timothy of the sincere faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5).
Paul writes that when he was downcast in Macedonia, God consoled him by the arrival of Titus with good news from Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:5–7).
Later Acts of Timothy relate that he was beaten to death at Ephesus for speaking against an idolatrous festival. The account is late and uncertain.
quotes: Let no one despise your youth, but set the believers an example in speech and conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
St Paul to Timothy, 1 Timothy 4:12
timothytitus.prayer: O God, who adorned Sts Timothy and Titus with apostolic virtues, grant, through their intercession, that, living justly and devoutly in this present age, we may merit to reach our heavenly homeland. Amen.

points: Grandmothers and mothers pass on the faith.
Stir up the gift of God within you.
homily: Dear friends, the day after the Conversion of St Paul, the Church remembers two of his closest helpers, Timothy and Titus. Timothy was young, perhaps shy, and Paul loved him as a son. Titus was a Gentile convert who became Paul's trusted messenger.

Where did Timothy's faith come from? Paul tells us: from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Let us thank God today for the grandmothers and mothers who taught us to pray. They are the first missionaries in every family.

Paul writes to Timothy: rekindle the gift of God that is within you (2 Timothy 1:6). Every one of us has received a gift in Baptism and Confirmation, and priests in ordination. Like a fire, it must be stirred up, or it grows cold.

Titus was sent to difficult places: to a quarrelling church in Corinth and to the island of Crete. He brought peace and order. Let us ask Sts Timothy and Titus to help us keep our faith alive, to pass it on to our children, and to be faithful helpers of our pastors. Amen.

cyrilathanasius.n: Mar Athanasius and Mar Cyril of Alexandria
cyrilathanasius.t: Patriarchs of Alexandria, defenders of the faith, Doctors of the Church
word: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John 1:1
life: On 18 January the Syriac tradition honours together two great bishops of Alexandria in Egypt, Athanasius and Cyril. A century apart, both defended the same truth: that Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, is truly God, the eternal Word made flesh for our salvation.

Athanasius was born around 296 in Alexandria. As a young deacon he accompanied his bishop Alexander to the Council of Nicaea in 325, which professed that the Son is of one substance with the Father against the teaching of Arius. In 328 he became bishop of Alexandria. Because he would not compromise the faith of Nicaea, he was driven into exile five times by emperors and opponents, spending about seventeen years away from his flock. He wrote On the Incarnation, the Life of St Antony, and in his Easter letter of 367 he listed the twenty-seven books of the New Testament as we have them today. He died on 2 May 373.

Cyril, born around 376, was the nephew of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and succeeded him in 412. His early years as bishop were marked by harsh conflicts in the city, including the murder of the philosopher Hypatia by a Christian mob in 415; historians still debate how far Cyril bore responsibility. His great service came later, when Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople, objected to calling Mary Theotokos, Mother of God. Cyril defended the title, because the child born of Mary is the one divine Person of the Word. The Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed this faith, and in 433 Cyril was reconciled with the bishops of Antioch. He died in 444.

Both are Doctors of the Church. Athanasius and Cyril are names often taken by bishops of the Syriac and Malankara traditions, a sign of how much these two teachers of the Incarnation are loved in our Church.
lessons: Jesus is truly God
The faith of Nicaea is the faith of our Creed.
Mary, Mother of God
Honouring Mary protects the truth about her Son.
Faithful in exile
Athanasius suffered rather than betray the truth.
Truth and charity together
Cyril's story shows that zeal needs to be joined to love and reconciliation.
stories: Athanasius was sent away from Alexandria five times between 335 and 366. Each time he returned, and his people welcomed him back.
A later saying describes him as Athanasius against the world, because for a time it seemed that almost everyone in power had abandoned the faith of Nicaea, while he held firm.
When the Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed that Mary is Mother of God, the people of Ephesus are said to have escorted the bishops through the streets with torches and rejoicing.
quotes: He became man that we might become God.
St Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54, in substance
p
cyrilathanasius.prayer: Lord God, you gave your Church Mar Athanasius and Mar Cyril as faithful witnesses to the divinity of your Son and to the honour of His Mother; through their prayers keep us firm in the true faith and make us one in love. Amen.

points: What we say of Mary protects what we believe of Jesus.
The Ninevite fast calls us to faith that changes life.
homily: Dear friends, today, on the first day of the fast of the Ninevites, our Church remembers two great bishops of Alexandria, Mar Athanasius and Mar Cyril. They lived a hundred years apart, but they defended the same truth: Jesus Christ is truly God.

St John begins his Gospel: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). Athanasius held to this faith of Nicaea through five exiles. He taught that the Son of God became man so that we might share in the life of God.

Cyril defended the title Mother of God for Mary. He was not simply praising Mary; he was protecting the truth that the child in her arms is God the Son. When we call Mary Theotokos, we confess who Jesus is.

As we keep the Ninevite fast, let us not only fast from food, but turn our minds and hearts to the truth of Christ. When we pray the Creed in the Holy Qurbono, let us say it slowly and with love, thanking God for these teachers of the faith. Amen.

macarios.t: Monk and father of the desert of Scetis, Egypt
word: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
Matthew 5:8
life: Macarius, often called Macarius the Great or Macarius the Egyptian, was born around 300 in a village of Upper Egypt. Early accounts say that as a young man he earned his living as a camel driver carrying natron, a kind of salt, before he gave himself to a life of prayer.

Around the age of thirty he withdrew into solitude, and about 330 he went deep into the desert of Scetis, the Wadi el-Natrun west of the Nile delta. According to the early monastic sources, he visited St Antony, the father of monks, and learned from him. Disciples gathered around Macarius, and Scetis became one of the great centres of monastic life. He was ordained a priest.

He was known for his humility, gentleness and long prayer, and the Sayings of the Desert Fathers preserve many of his words. According to the historians of the time, during the Arian persecution under Valens he was briefly exiled to an island in the Nile. He died around 390, at about ninety years of age. The monastery that bears his name, Deir Abu Maqar, still stands in the Egyptian desert.

A collection of Fifty Spiritual Homilies on the work of the Holy Spirit in the heart has long been attributed to him; most scholars now think they were written later by a Syrian monk, but they reflect the spirit of the desert and are loved in East and West.
lessons: Humility conquers
Macarius overcame evil by lowliness, not by force.
Prayer of the heart
A short prayer, repeated with faith, can fill the whole day.
Purity of heart
Fasting and silence serve to make the heart clear for God.
Gentleness
He corrected others with kindness.
stories: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers tell that the devil said to Macarius: whatever you do, I do also; you fast, I never eat; you keep vigil, I never sleep; in one thing only you overcome me, your humility.
When monks asked him how to pray, Macarius told them they need not use many words; it is enough to stretch out the hands and say: Lord, as you will and as you know, have mercy.

The Sayings tell that as a young hermit Macarius was falsely accused of wronging a village girl. He did not defend himself, but worked to support her. When the truth came out, the villagers came to ask his pardon, and he withdrew to Scetis.
quotes: Lord, as you will and as you know, have mercy.
Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Macarius 19, in substance
p
macarios.prayer: Lord God, you led Mar Macarios into the desert to seek your face in silence and humility; through his prayers give us pure hearts, a spirit of prayer and true repentance. Amen.

points: Fasting clears the heart to see God (Matthew 5:8).
The devil could not imitate his humility.
homily: Dear friends, on this second day of the fast of the Ninevites we remember Mar Macarios, one of the great fathers of the Egyptian desert. He was once a camel driver; he became a man of prayer whose wisdom drew disciples from far and wide.

Jesus says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God (Matthew 5:8). Macarius went into the desert not to escape people, but to let God purify his heart. Fasting, silence and work were his ways of making room for God.

The Sayings of the Desert Fathers tell that the devil once complained to him: you fast, but I never eat; you keep vigil, but I never sleep; only your humility defeats me. Our fasts mean little without humility. The people of Nineveh did not only fast; they humbled themselves and turned from evil.

Macarius taught a very simple prayer: Lord, as you will and as you know, have mercy. During these days of fasting, let us repeat it often, at work, on the road and before sleep, and come to the Holy Qurbono with humble and pure hearts. Amen.

angelamerici.t: Virgin, foundress of the Company of St Ursula
word: there is need of only one thing. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.
Luke 10:42
life: Angela Merici was born around 1474 at Desenzano, on Lake Garda in northern Italy. She lost both her parents while still young and went to live with an uncle at Salò. She became a Franciscan tertiary and gave herself to prayer, fasting and care for the poor.

In 1516 she moved to Brescia, where she became known as a woman of wisdom whom many people, rich and poor, came to for counsel. In 1524 she went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, and in the Jubilee year 1525 she visited Rome, where, according to her early biographers, Pope Clement VII invited her to stay; she preferred to return to Brescia.

She saw that many young women had no access to Christian formation and could neither enter a convent nor find a good marriage. On 25 November 1535 she founded with twenty-eight companions the Company of St Ursula: women consecrated to Christ who lived in their own homes, without enclosure, praying, serving and teaching the faith, especially to girls. It was a new form of consecrated life in the world.

Angela died at Brescia on 27 January 1540. After her death the Ursulines spread widely and, after the Council of Trent, many communities became religious congregations devoted to the education of girls, which they continue in many countries. Pope Pius VII canonised her in 1807.
lessons: Christ the one thing necessary
Angela's consecration was a choice of the better part.
Holiness in ordinary places
Her companions served God in their own homes and towns.
Educating girls
She saw the dignity of young women and their need for formation.
Gentle leadership
She asked her leaders to guide with love, not harshness.
stories: Her early biographers tell that as a young woman, while working in the fields, she saw a vision of a ladder reaching to heaven with young women ascending it, and understood that she would one day found a company of consecrated women.
Blind on the way to Jerusalem
According to the early accounts, Angela lost her sight on the voyage to the Holy Land, visited the holy places in blindness, and recovered her sight on the way home.
On 25 November 1535, in a small house beside the church of St Afra in Brescia, Angela and twenty-eight young women consecrated themselves to God in the Company of St Ursula.
angelamerici.prayer: Lord Jesus, St Angela Merici chose you as the one thing necessary and served you in the young; through her prayers help us to choose the better part, and bless all who teach and form the young in faith. Amen.

points: Like Mary of Bethany, Angela chose Jesus first (Luke 10:42).
Holiness can grow in ordinary homes.
Education is a work of love.
homily: Dear friends, St Angela Merici was a laywoman of northern Italy who, early in the sixteenth century, saw a great need: many young women had no one to form them in the faith. She did not wait for others to act.

In the Gospel Jesus tells Martha that there is need of only one thing, and that Mary has chosen the better part (Luke 10:42). Angela chose that better part: Jesus Christ above all. From that choice came her service.

In 1535 she gathered young women who consecrated their lives to Christ while living in their own homes, praying, serving and teaching. It was something new in the Church. Later the Ursulines became teachers of girls in many lands.

Let us thank God today for all women religious and teachers who form young people in faith and knowledge. And let us ask St Angela to help us choose the better part, and to serve Christ wherever we live. Amen.

thomasaquinas.t: Dominican priest, theologian, Doctor of the Church
word: Therefore I prayed, and understanding was given me; I called on God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me.
Wisdom 7:7
life: Thomas was born around 1225 in the castle of Roccasecca, between Rome and Naples, into a noble family of the Aquino line. At about five years of age he was sent to the great Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, and later studied at the university of Naples, where he came to know the new Order of Preachers founded by St Dominic.

In 1244 he entered the Dominicans. His family, who hoped he would become abbot of Monte Cassino, had him seized on the road and kept at home for about a year, but he did not change his mind. He then studied under St Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne.

Thomas became a master of theology at Paris and taught there and in Italy. With great clarity he showed that faith and reason do not contradict each other, since both come from God, and he used the philosophy of Aristotle in the service of the faith. His greatest work, the Summa Theologiae, explains the whole of Catholic doctrine. According to a tradition accepted by most scholars, at the request of Pope Urban IV he composed the texts for the new feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, whose hymns are still sung today.

On 6 December 1273, after an experience during the celebration of the Eucharist, he stopped writing. Summoned to the Council of Lyons, he fell ill on the way and died at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova on 7 March 1274. He was canonised in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567. His memorial is kept on 28 January, the day his relics were brought to Toulouse in 1369. He is the patron of Catholic schools and students.
lessons: Faith and reason
Truth is one, because God is its source.
Study as prayer
Thomas prayed before he studied and wrote.
Humility of the learned
The greatest theologian of his age called his work straw before the mystery of God.
Love for the Eucharist
His hymns teach us to adore.
stories: His fellow students, it is said, called the large, silent Thomas the dumb ox. St Albert the Great replied that one day the bellowing of this ox would be heard throughout the world.

His early biographers tell that while he was praying before a crucifix in Naples, Christ said to him: you have written well of me, Thomas; what reward would you have? He answered: nothing but yourself, Lord.

After the experience of 6 December 1273, according to testimony given at his canonisation, Thomas told his companion Reginald that all he had written seemed to him like straw compared with what he had seen.
quotes: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.
St Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 8, in substance
p
thomasaquinas.prayer: Lord God, source of all truth, you gave St Thomas Aquinas a mind that sought you and a heart that adored you; through his prayers help us to study with humility, to love the truth, and to find our reward in you alone. Amen.

points: Our faith is reasonable and beautiful.
All learning ends in love and adoration.
homily: Dear friends, St Thomas Aquinas was one of the greatest minds the Church has ever known. Yet as a student he was so quiet that his companions called him the dumb ox. His teacher, St Albert the Great, saw more deeply.

Thomas always prayed before he studied. Like Solomon he could say: Therefore I prayed, and understanding was given me (Wisdom 7:7). He showed that faith and reason are friends, because both come from the one God who is Truth.

His great Summa explains the whole faith with clarity and order. But he also wrote hymns to Christ in the Eucharist, which the Church still sings. His learning led him to adoration. Near the end of his life he said that all he had written seemed like straw compared with what God had shown him.
Today let us pray for students and teachers, and ask St Thomas to help us love the truth, study with humility, and say with him: nothing but you, Lord. Amen.

ignatiusnoorono.n: St Ignatius of Antioch (Mar Ignatius Noorono)
word: Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
John 12:24
life: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch in Syria, the city where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26). According to the historian Eusebius, he was the third bishop there, after St Peter and Evodius. He also called himself Theophoros, God-bearer, and the Syriac tradition names him Noorono, the fiery one.

Under the emperor Trajan he was arrested and taken under military guard to Rome to be thrown to wild beasts. On the journey through Asia Minor, at Smyrna and Troas, he wrote seven letters: to the Churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia and Smyrna, and to St Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna. These letters are among the most precious writings of the early Church.

In them Ignatius urges Christians to stay united with their bishop, presbyters and deacons, and to gather around the one Eucharist, which he calls the medicine of immortality. He defends the true humanity of Christ against those who said that He only seemed to suffer. He is the first known writer to use the expression the Catholic Church. To the Christians of Rome he begged that they not try to save him from martyrdom.

He died in Rome around the year 107, torn by beasts in the arena. The Latin Church keeps his memorial on 17 October; the Malankara Church remembers him on 29 January. The patriarchs of Antioch in the Syriac tradition take the name Ignatius in his honour.
lessons: United with the bishop
Ignatius saw the unity of the Church gathered around the bishop and the Eucharist.
The medicine of immortality
The Eucharist is the food of eternal life.
Fiery love
He longed to be with Christ more than to live.
Christ truly suffered
Our salvation is real, because His flesh was real.
stories: To the Romans Ignatius wrote that he was God's wheat, to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that he might be found the pure bread of Christ.
He describes his guards as ten leopards, who grew worse the more kindly they were treated, and says he was learning discipleship through their ill treatment.
The child Jesus took in his arms
A later legend says that Ignatius was the child whom Jesus took in his arms and set among the disciples (Mark 9:36). There is no evidence for this.
quotes: I am the wheat of God, and am ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.
St Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Romans 4
p
ignatiusnoorono.prayer: Lord God, you made St Ignatius of Antioch burn with love for your Son even to martyrdom; through his prayers help us to love the unity of your Church, to hunger for the Bread of Life, and to give our lives for you. Amen.

points: Unity around the bishop and the altar.
homily: Dear friends, St Ignatius was bishop of Antioch, the city where the followers of Jesus were first called Christians. Around the year 107 he was arrested and taken to Rome to die in the arena.

On the way he wrote seven letters. He begged the Christians of Rome not to save him, saying he was God's wheat, to be ground by the teeth of beasts to become the pure bread of Christ. He had understood the words of Jesus: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24).

In his letters Ignatius asks Christians to remain united with their bishop and to gather around the one Eucharist, which he calls the medicine of immortality. Division weakens the Church; unity around Christ makes it strong.
Let us ask St Ignatius for his fiery love: love for Christ, love for the Eucharist, love for the unity of the Church. And let us pray for Christians who are persecuted for their faith today. Amen.

aphrahat.n: Mar Jacob Aphrahat, the Persian Sage
word: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
Matthew 7:24
life: Aphrahat lived in the fourth century in the Persian Empire, beyond the eastern frontier of Rome, and is called the Persian Sage. He is the earliest Syriac Father whose major writings have come down to us. We know very little about his life: he was certainly a teacher of high standing in the Church, and Syriac tradition remembers him as a monk and bishop. The name Jacob is attached to him only in later tradition.

Between 337 and 345 he wrote twenty-three Demonstrations, the first twenty-two following the letters of the Syriac alphabet. They speak of faith, love, fasting, prayer, humility, repentance, the resurrection, and the life of the sons and daughters of the covenant, men and women who dedicated themselves to God within the Church.

He wrote during the persecution of Christians by the Persian king Shapur II, which began around 340, and he encouraged the faithful to remain firm. His language is close to the Bible and to the Semitic world of Jesus. He teaches that faith is a house built on the rock who is Christ, and that the heart of the believer is a temple where Christ dwells.
He died around 345. He is honoured in the Syriac Churches as a holy teacher, and his Demonstrations are still read as a witness to the early faith of Christians in the East.
lessons: Built on the rock
Faith is a house whose foundation is Christ.
The heart as a temple
Christ dwells in a pure heart.
Firm in persecution
He strengthened Christians under Shapur II.
Prayer from a pure heart
Purity of heart makes prayer true.
stories: Aphrahat arranged his first twenty-two Demonstrations so that each begins with a letter of the Syriac alphabet in order, from Olaph to Tau, a whole alphabet of instruction in the faith.
In his first Demonstration, on faith, Aphrahat describes faith as a building whose foundation is the rock, Christ, and on which the believer builds with good works.
quotes: Purity of heart is prayer, more than all the prayers that are uttered with the mouth.
Mar Aphrahat, Demonstration 4, On Prayer, in substance
p
aphrahat.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, rock of our faith, through the prayers of Mar Jacob Aphrahat, make our hearts your temple, our words true and kind, and our lives a house built on you. Amen.

points: Christ wants to dwell in us.
A pure heart is the best preparation for Great Lent.
homily: Dear friends, today the Syriac tradition remembers Mar Jacob Aphrahat, the Persian Sage, who lived in the fourth century in the Persian Empire. He is the earliest Syriac Father whose writings have reached us, and he wrote at a time when Christians there were persecuted.

Aphrahat loved the words of Jesus: everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock (Matthew 7:24). For him faith is a house, and Christ is its foundation. Our good works are the stones we build on that rock.
He also taught that the heart is a temple where Christ wishes to dwell, and that true prayer begins with a pure heart. Words alone are not enough; a heart that forgives and loves is itself a prayer.

Great Lent is near. Let us examine our hearts, as Aphrahat urged, and prepare a clean temple for Christ, so that our fasting, our prayer and our participation in the Holy Qurbono may come from a heart built on the rock. Amen.

johnbosco.t: Priest, father and teacher of the young, founder of the Salesians
word: Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.
Matthew 18:5
life: John Bosco was born on 16 August 1815 at Becchi, near Castelnuovo d'Asti in Piedmont, northern Italy, into a poor farming family. His father died when he was not yet two, and his mother, Margaret Occhiena, raised her sons with deep faith. John had to work hard and struggled for years to be able to study.

He was ordained a priest in Turin in 1841. The city was growing fast with factories, and many boys from the countryside lived on the streets, worked in harsh conditions or ended up in prison. Don Bosco, as he came to be called, gathered them on Sundays for games, catechism and prayer. This Oratory, named after St Francis de Sales, found a permanent home at Valdocco in 1846. He opened workshops and schools, and his mother came to live there as a mother to the boys.

His way of education, which he called the preventive system, rested on reason, religion and loving kindness: the educator stays among the young, wins their trust and prevents evil rather than only punishing it. In 1859 he founded the Salesian Society, and in 1872, with St Mary Domenica Mazzarello, the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians. He built the Basilica of Mary Help of Christians in Turin and sent missionaries to South America. Among his pupils was St Dominic Savio.

Don Bosco died in Turin on 31 January 1888. Pope Pius XI canonised him on Easter Sunday 1934. The Salesians came to India in 1906, and today in Kerala and across the country their schools, technical institutes and homes for children at risk continue his work.
lessons: Love that the young can feel
Don Bosco wanted young people to know that they were loved.
Prevention, not only punishment
Reason, faith and kindness form good Christians and honest citizens.
Joy and holiness
Holiness can be cheerful.
Trust in Mary
He did everything under the protection of Mary Help of Christians.
stories: In his Memoirs Don Bosco tells of a dream he had at about nine years old: a crowd of fighting boys, a majestic man who told him to win them not with blows but with gentleness, and a lady who showed him wild animals turning into lambs. He understood it later as his life's mission.
As a boy, according to his Memoirs, John learned juggling and rope tricks to draw the village children together; after the show he would repeat the Sunday sermon and lead them in prayer.
Stories told by Don Bosco and his companions speak of a large grey dog that appeared when he was in danger on the streets of Turin and protected him, then disappeared.
quotes: It is not enough to love the young; they must know that they are loved.
St John Bosco, Letter from Rome, 1884, in substance

johnbosco.prayer: Lord God, in St John Bosco you gave the young a father and a friend; through his prayers give us patience, joy and kindness with children and young people, and help us to lead them to Christ. Amen.

points: Whoever welcomes a child welcomes Christ (Matthew 18:5).
A way of education for families and schools.
She did it all, he said.
homily: Dear friends, St John Bosco grew up poor, lost his father as a baby and had to fight to get an education. When he became a priest in Turin, he saw boys living on the streets, exploited in workshops and locked in prisons, and he decided to give his life to them.

Jesus said: Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me (Matthew 18:5). Don Bosco welcomed thousands. He played with them, taught them a trade, heard their confessions and led them to Christ. His way was reason, religion and loving kindness.

He used to say that it is not enough to love the young; they must know that they are loved. Parents, teachers and priests can ask themselves: do the young people around me feel loved? Do they find in us patience and joy?

Let us pray today for the children and youth of our families and parishes, especially those in danger or without care. May St John Bosco and Mary Help of Christians, whom he loved so much, guide them to Christ. Amen.

jude.t: One of the Twelve, patron of difficult and desperate causes; feast kept with St Simon the Zealot
word: But you, beloved, build yourselves up on your most holy faith; pray in the Holy Spirit; keep yourselves in the love of God; look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.
Jude 20–21
life: Jude was one of the twelve apostles whom Jesus chose after spending the whole night in prayer on the mountain (Luke 6:12–16). Luke calls him “Judas son of James”; Matthew and Mark name, in the same place in their lists, an apostle called Thaddaeus, and the Church has long understood these to be the same man. That is why he is known as Jude Thaddeus. The Gospels take care to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord.

John's Gospel keeps one question of his, asked at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” (John 14:22). Jesus answered that the Father and the Son will come and make their home with everyone who loves him and keeps his word (John 14:23). After the Ascension, Jude was with Mary and the other apostles in the upper room, devoted to prayer as they waited for the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:13–14).

The short Letter of Jude in the New Testament is written by “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (Jude 1). Tradition has attributed it to the apostle; some scholars think of another Jude, a relative of the Lord. The letter urges Christians to “contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to the saints” (Jude 3), asks mercy for those who waver, and ends with one of the most beautiful hymns of praise in the Bible (Jude 24–25).

According to ancient tradition, Jude preached the Gospel in Mesopotamia and Persia together with Simon the Zealot, and both died as martyrs there. This is why the Roman calendar keeps their feast together on 28 October. Their relics are venerated in St Peter's Basilica in Rome. In art Jude is usually shown with a club, an axe or a halberd, the instrument of his martyrdom according to tradition, and often with a medallion bearing the face of Christ.

Popular devotion has made him the patron of difficult and desperate causes. A common explanation is that, because his name sounded like the traitor's, Christians for centuries seldom prayed to him, so that he came to be invoked when every other help seemed to have failed. In Kerala, as in many parts of the world, great crowds come to his shrines and to the weekly novena in his honor, bringing their burdens of sickness, debt, unemployment and family trouble.
lessons: An apostle who asked
Jude's one recorded question led Jesus to promise that God makes his home in those who love him (John 14:22–23).
Hidden but faithful
Little is written about him, yet he gave his whole life. Holiness does not need fame.
Guard the faith, show mercy
His letter asks us to contend for the faith and to have mercy on those who waver (Jude 3, 22).
No cause is hopeless with God
True devotion to Jude leads us to Christ, for nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37).
stories: The question at the Last Supper

On the night before he died, Jesus spoke of showing himself to his disciples. Jude asked why only to them and not to the whole world. Jesus answered that the Father and he would come and make their home in everyone who loves him and keeps his word (John 14:22–23).
The face of Christ sent to Edessa

An ancient legend tells that King Abgar of Edessa, who was sick, wrote to Jesus asking him to come and heal him. After the Ascension, a disciple named Thaddaeus was sent to him; the king was healed and many in Edessa believed. Eusebius records an early form of the story in the fourth century; later versions add that Thaddaeus carried a cloth bearing the face of Christ. The story is legendary, but it explains why St Jude is so often shown with the face of Christ on his breast.

Devotion to St Jude spread widely in later centuries. It is often said that St Bridget of Sweden (fourteenth century) was told in prayer to turn to him with great confidence. Ever since, people who had lost hope have prayed to him, and many have given thanks for help received. That is why so many newspapers carry small notes of thanks to St Jude.
quotes: Now to him who is able to keep you from falling, and to make you stand without blemish in the presence of his glory with rejoicing, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, power, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
Jude 24–25
Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?
St Jude, John 14:22
The Letter of Jude invites us to live our faith with coherence, building ourselves up in it and praying in the Holy Spirit.
